prisma-calibration/technical-reference/s.title: Spline model fitting (v1)
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/s.content:
In one sentence: “Color Model v1” is the server’s label for the legacy-spline model — a per-filament monotone PCHIP transmission profile built by fit_spline_profile (calibration.fitting.fitting), predicted and stacked by predict/compose (calibration.fitting.composition), and installed through the staged run_legacy_spline_fit_all path reached by both the unified workflow and /api/profiles/fit-all — while the notebook-era batch_fit.py / fitter_core.py / strip_loader.py / export.py chain sits off the live fit path.

This page maps the code of the v1 fitter: the modules, the data flow from sample to profile, how a stacked appearance is predicted, and how its two public callers converge on one internal current-fit boundary. The older code names this boundary “publication”; it does not create or change a Generator library. It deliberately does not re-derive the physics — why PCHIP, what an optical-density transmission curve is, or what pair corrections compensate for. For the model form and math — including the empirical two-filament pair corrections — read Color Model v1. For where a v1 fit sits in the operator workflow, see Model workflow, publication, and review and The Modeling page.
Related: calibration.fitting.fitting · calibration.fitting.legacy_spline_fit_job · calibration.fitting.composition · calibration.fitting.color_math · calibration.fitting.fitter_core · calibration.fitting.batch_fit · calibration.fitting.strip_loader · calibration.fitting.export
”Color Model v1” is the legacy-spline model
The UI and persistence layer call this the legacy-spline model. The server’s three current-fit kinds are gated by sqlite_data_access._MODEL_KINDS; a v1 fit is recorded under model_kind="legacy_spline". Wherever the interface says “Color Model v1,” the code says legacy_spline. Everything on this page produces or consumes that artifact set: per-filament profile JSONs plus a single pair_corrections.json.
The live core is calibration.fitting.fitting (fitting.py). Its module header retains the historical names batch_fit_spline.py and model_spline.py for the logic folded into this UI-driven module. Those filenames no longer exist as standalone modules. The live fit paths call fitting.py; retained notebook-origin support modules are described in the last section and sit outside the production fitting route except for the explicitly identified pair-correction helpers.
The spline profile — build, predict, serialize
A v1 profile is a plain dict: knots_mm (thicknesses, first knot 0.0) plus per-channel T_r/T_g/T_b transmission arrays, tagged model: 'spline'. The primitives that operate on it:

build_spline constructs three PchipInterpolators (one per channel), asserting the first knot is at d=0 and clipping T to [0,1].
predict evaluates a profile at thickness d, returning a linear-RGB T triple; below d=0 it returns ones, and beyond the last knot it hands off to _extrapolate, a log-linear extension. The why of that extrapolation belongs to Color Model v1.
to_srgb gamma-encodes linear T for display; profile_from_dict pre-builds and caches the interpolators; profile_to_save_dict strips the non-serializable _splines object and staleness flags before JSON write.
save_profile / load_profile write/read {profiles_dir}/{fid}.json. Loading routes through _load_fresh_profile_path, which treats any profile carrying a stale/stale_reason/stale_at flag as missing through _profile_is_stale — a stale profile is never silently used.

OKLab conversion (linear_to_oklab) and deltaE_ok live here too and back the fit-quality diagnostics.
From sample to strip dict — the adapters
The fitter’s internal unit is a strip dict (thicknesses, per-swatch linear transmission, optional fixed_layers). Adapters convert a live Sample into that shape:

_legacy_spline_geometry reads a sample’s canonical physical stack (via physical_stack_for_swatch, calibration.fitting.physical_stack) and returns the one variable filament plus any fixed base layers below it — or None for richer geometries the legacy spline deliberately refuses to reinterpret (is_legacy_spline_supported_stack).
_sample_to_strip_dict is the legacy adapter reading color from Sample.measurements. _sample_to_strip_dict_from_sidecar is its production twin, pulling measured transmission and I0 from the per-sample extraction_result sidecar while keeping geometry and filament assignments from the live sample; a measurement-bearing sample with an absent or malformed sidecar raises SidecarAdapterError rather than falling back.
The active source is the module switch _MEASURED_SOURCE = "sidecar"; _strip_dict_for dispatches on it, and use_measured_source is a context manager for oracle/rollback/test runs. Production reads the sidecar.

_load_strips_from_samples and _load_all_strips_from_samples walk store.list_samples(), keep only processed samples with measurements and a strip definition, and bucket the resulting strip dicts by variable filament. In the production SQLite store, Sample.measurements is projected only from an accepted extraction result. Pending-review extractions therefore fail this gate even though the fitting helpers do not repeat an explicit review_accepted test. The fit paths pass the pre-built strips_by_filament cache down so the whole corpus is loaded once per run.
The four data sources and the fit
For each filament, four loaders extract (d, T_rgb) points, each targeting a different strip geometry:

load_single_fil_data — solo strips (“thick”), skipping colored-base and white-base strips.
load_thin_strip_data — white-base + overlay strips (“thin”), peeling the base by local d=0 normalization (_d0_normalize_strip).
load_fixed_role_data — Role-B cross-cal, where the filament is the fixed base and a d=0 swatch is a direct profile-independent measurement of it.
load_crosscal_data — Role-A cross-cal (filament is the variable overlay on a colored base), T0-weighted; diagnostic-only for fitting.

fit_spline_profile is the core. It merges the caller’s exclusions with the hardwired EXCLUDED_EXPERIMENTS (still pinning exp-135 pending its per-sample migration) and the always-on registry-driven samples_excluded_by_filament set. It then combines sources by priority (thick baseline, thin fills gaps and wins below thin_wins_below; combine_datasets), drops outlier knots against a log-linear neighbor trend (_drop_outlier_knots_with_removed), prepends the d=0/T=1 anchor, enforces per-channel monotone non-increase, applies a T_FLOOR of 0.003, and truncates a trailing noise floor. It returns (profile_dict, diagnostics_dict) — (None, diagnostics) on failure with an error key. get_fit_data_points and compute_delta_e expose the same data for the review charts.
Predicting stacked appearance and pair corrections
calibration.fitting.composition (composition.py) predicts what a stack of layers looks like. compose multiplies each layer’s predict(profile, d) per channel, then — if a corrections table is supplied and there are ≥2 layers — applies an interpolated per-pair factor keyed overlay_fid|base@d through _interpolate_correction. predict_two_layer is the direct overlay-plus-base convenience path using calibration.fitting.color_math’s interp_single. calibration.fitting.color_math is a pure-math leaf (no intra-project imports) that is genuinely live — imported by both composition.py and the server. compute_sample_predictions drives compose over every processed sample of a filament to build the predicted-vs-measured review payload.
The pair corrections themselves are computed on the live path by compute_and_save_pair_corrections: it builds a registry with _build_pair_corrections_registry, then calls into calibration.fitting.fitter_core for compute_pair_corrections and save_pair_corrections, writing pair_corrections.json beside the profiles. This is the one live thread through the notebook-origin fitter_core — its correction math is reused, but its strip-file fitting is not. When a full model library is explicitly published, Generator reads the copied correction file from its selected immutable library at LUT build time; what the corrections model is covered by Color Model v1’s pair-corrections section.
The two entry points share one staged publisher
Both live entry points converge on run_legacy_spline_fit_all and the same staged publisher:


Unified workflow → calibration.fitting.legacy_spline_fit_job. run_legacy_spline_fit_all creates a private .legacy-spline-fit-<uuid> workspace for SQLite publication. The implementation fits every target it can, deletes staged profiles that did not fit successfully, computes pair corrections when at least one profile fitted, and calls publish_staged_legacy_spline_fit when fitted > 0 and pair-correction generation succeeded. Despite the “legacy” name this module is live and is called by the unified model-fit workflow.


Direct /fit-all routes → calibration.server. The synchronous and asynchronous endpoints call _run_profile_fit_all, whose implementation wraps _run_legacy_spline_fit_all(..., publish=True). The direct API is therefore a second entry into the same fitter and publication boundary, not a separately maintained fitting implementation. The retained per-profile and fit-all browser commands live in app/features/modeling/profiles.js, but the current Modeling mode is owned by app/features/modeling/review.js (renderModelsView); the ordinary UI enters the unified Fit Models flow through app/features/modeling/workflow.js.


The important qualification is that swap atomicity is not all-filament success. If one filament fit fails but another succeeds, the successful subset can replace the current v1 artifact set and receive a new model_fit_id. The unified workflow then notices the nonzero failed count, reports the overall operation as failed, records partial_publication.legacy_spline = true, and stops before v2. A pair-correction failure prevents publication entirely.
publish_staged_legacy_spline_fit swaps the staged profiles and pair corrections into the live paths before publishing SQLite. If an ordinary database-publication exception occurs, it restores the previous files; if that rollback is itself incomplete, it raises a distinct error and preserves surviving .rollback-* copies for manual recovery. Successful publication records the new artifact set, deletes the prior fit row and children, and removes the temporary rollback copies.
That compensation does not make the multi-step filesystem/SQLite transition process-kill atomic. A hard stop between its directory/pair swaps and SQLite replacement can leave missing or mixed live artifacts, rollback copies, or new files paired with the old database record. There is no startup journal that completes or reverses this v1 transition. Do not kill Calibration while Fit Models is publishing; after an abnormal stop, verify all three model statuses and publication readiness before trusting the working set.
Notebook-origin modules off the live path
fitting.py was ported from an earlier strip-file pipeline. Parts of that notebook-origin pipeline still ship under the current filenames below, but they are not what the live fit runs:

calibration.fitting.batch_fit (batch_fit.py) is the original batch_fit_spline.py: it reads pre-materialized strip files from STRIPS_DIR, prints progress, and has a __main__ main(). Its own fit_spline_profile is the direct ancestor of fitting.fit_spline_profile. It has no intra-project imports and is imported only by fitter_core; on the live pair-correction path it is loaded as a side effect but its fitting functions are never invoked. Strip files are themselves legacy — the live fitter reads samples directly.
calibration.fitting.fitter_core (fitter_core.py) wraps batch_fit for the notebook fitter through fit_profile and load_all_data. Only its pair-correction helpers (compute_pair_corrections, save_pair_corrections) are live-reachable, pulled in lazily by fitting.compute_and_save_pair_corrections; the rest is notebook/CLI surface. It is imported by calibration.fitting.export.
calibration.fitting.strip_loader (strip_loader.py) builds a filament-to-strips registry by scanning strip-file JSONs through load_strip_registry; it is self-described as extracted from 01_fitter.ipynb/02_composer.ipynb and imported only by export.
calibration.fitting.export (export.py, originally fitter_json_export.py) turns fitter results into REST-serializable dicts through export_transmission_curve and export_filament_summary, replacing the notebook’s matplotlib output. Its Architecture node lists no importers — it is not wired into the live server graph.

The heavy numerical photo-stack model referenced by the v2 pages lives in the shared lib.photo_stack_model.*, not here; this page’s modules are strictly the v1 legacy-spline path.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.title: The camera transform fitter
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.content:
In one sentence: run_camera_transform_build_job (calibration.fitting.camera_transform.job) builds a corpus of (transmission → embedded-JPEG appearance) pairs, validates with deterministic five-fold sample-grouped cross-validation, refits on all clean evidence, bakes the numeric inverse into a 3D LUT, and writes a staged generation that the shared publication boundary coordinates with SQLite before retiring the old generation.

This page is the code-level map of the module cluster under calibration/fitting/camera_transform/: how a Camera Transform artifact is built. The model form it fits — the root-polynomial feature map, the per-channel monotone PCHIP curves, F (fitted transmission → appearance) and its numeric inverse G baked as a LUT — is derived in The Camera Transform; this page links it rather than re-deriving it. The distinction between the transmission the corpus reads and the appearance it targets is Transmission vs Appearance. The shared model runtime that both the fitter and the generator import is lib.camera_transform. How this build job is dispatched alongside the other model fits, and how its output is published, is Model workflow, publication, and review.
Here, the older internal “publication” names mean coordinated replacement of Calibration’s current working Camera Transform. They do not create or update a Generator library; that requires the separate user-facing Publish Models action after all three working fits are current.
Related: calibration.fitting.camera_transform.job · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.corpus · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fit · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.lut · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.export · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fingerprint · calibration.fitting.camera_transform.parity · lib.camera_transform
The build job — five phases, two gates
run_camera_transform_build_job is the single entry point. It is called by both the unified workflow and the server’s standalone Camera Transform job: its Imported by list is calibration.fitting.model_fit_workflow and calibration.server. It takes a store, an optional output_dir (default store.root / "camera_transform"), and a use_fit_exclusions flag (default False; the production webapp callers pass True); it emits five progress phases through an optional _emit callback.
The phases run in fixed order:

Corpus. build_camera_transform_corpus_from_extraction_results builds the (T, appearance) corpus from stored sidecars (see below). Alongside it, build_camera_transform_fit_fingerprint computes the robust fit-input fingerprint. An empty corpus raises RuntimeError; fewer than five eligible samples cannot support the validation policy; a corpus below MIN_USABLE_SWATCHES = 200 does not fail — it appends a “coverage is thin” warning and continues.
Fit. fit_camera_transform(corpus.rows) returns a CameraTransformFitResult.
Validate. The pooled out-of-fold mean dE76 is read from fit.metrics["validation"]["dE76_CIELAB"]["mean"]; if it exceeds MAX_VALIDATION_MEAN_DE76 = 6.0, the job raises RuntimeError and — crucially — the existing artifact is not modified. Nothing is written until this gate passes.
Bake. bake_inverse_lut(fit.params) produces the inverse LUT.
Export. write_camera_transform_artifact writes the payload, LUT, and manifest into a complete generation directory. Its activate=publish argument controls whether the writer also advances CURRENT; both production webapp callers pass publish=False and publish through publish_camera_transform_fit afterward.

Between bake and export the job assembles the payload and manifest. The manifest carries the corpus summary, pooled and per-fold out-of-fold CIELAB/OKLab metrics, final-fit training diagnostics, hygiene drop counts, the source_data_fingerprint, the params_sha256 identity hash, and the quality-gate thresholds and warnings. The return value reports status "warning" or "ok" and echoes the summary and manifest.
Stable identity hash across identical re-fits
_previous_params_sha256_if_same is a small but deliberate detail: before hashing the new payload it loads the existing artifact, and if the freshly fit params array is bit-for-bit equal to the stored one it reuses the prior params_sha256. So a rebuild that lands on identical parameters keeps its identity hash stable rather than minting a new one from an unrelated payload field.
The corpus — transmission paired with embedded-JPEG appearance
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.corpus builds the training table. Each row pairs a swatch’s transmission (T_R/T_G/T_B, the linear measured values) with its appearance (jpeg_r/g/b, median byte RGB from Canon’s embedded CR2 JPEG). The appearance target is the embedded JPEG render specifically — the module docstring is emphatic that it never falls back to the libraw visual render, thumbnails, or measurement medians, because those use per-image auto-brightening and different tone/hue rendering. This transmission-vs-appearance split is the whole point of the Camera Transform; see Transmission vs Appearance.
There are two builders, and only one is on the live path:

build_camera_transform_corpus_from_extraction_results is the live builder. It does not reopen source images at fit time. The live Sample controls which samples and swatches participate, their row order, fit_state, excluded_swatches, and variable_fid. For each participating swatch, the accepted extraction_result sidecar supplies the stored nominal thickness, measured transmission, embedded-JPEG appearance, appearance source, and extraction diagnostics. It fails loud via StoredCorpusError when a measurement-bearing sample is missing or has a malformed sidecar, when successful appearance diagnostics are incomplete, or when an included swatch lacks stored appearance — never a silent skip.
build_camera_transform_corpus is the older fit-time re-extraction path — it opens each CR2, locates the strip in the JPEG frame, and samples swatch boxes directly. It is aliased build_camera_transform_corpus_legacy_extract and is kept callable only for the parity oracle and tests; the job comment records it was retired from the fit path once a full-library parity oracle passed exact. Its geometry helpers still live here — _locate_strip, _compute_swatch_boxes, _box_median — and the fit-time and stored paths share _build_corpus_summary so their summaries stay identical.

Both builders return a frozen CameraTransformCorpus: the rows DataFrame, a summary dict, the skipped_samples list, and a source_fingerprint. _orient_colors correlates each swatch’s stored G_linear transmission against JPEG luminance (signed Spearman) and flips the swatch order if the reversed correlation is stronger; the resulting order_correlation is a per-sample extraction-quality guard, not a transmission-vs-thickness check. The legacy builder performs that work at fit time. On the production path it was already performed when the accepted extraction sidecar was created; the live corpus reads appearance_orientation_flipped and appearance_order_correlation back from that sidecar rather than recomputing them.
The live builder’s accepted-only boundary is enforced indirectly by the production SQLite sample projection. It checks for a processed sample with Sample.measurements; SQLite hydrates those measurements only from an accepted extraction result. Pending-review results therefore do not enter the corpus even though the corpus helper does not repeat a review_accepted predicate. The focused pending-review payload test covers this behavior.
The corpus module is imported beyond the fitter by calibration.maintenance_reextract, calibration.processing.extraction_result, and calibration.processing.extraction_visuals, which reuse its extraction helpers for re-extraction, sidecar production, and review visuals. calibration.maintenance reaches that behavior through the re-extraction workflow rather than importing the corpus module directly.
The fit — filter, cross-validate, refit
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fit holds fit_camera_transform and the numerical machinery around it. It runs three stages on the corpus rows:

Filter. load_and_filter applies five hygiene rules — drop fit_state == "excluded", drop whole samples whose order_correlation is below 0.8, drop physically suspicious bright/opaque rows, drop NaNs, and mark (but keep) JPEG-clipped rows so they are censored from the loss (JPEG_CLIP_THRESHOLD = 250). It returns the cleaned frame plus a drop_counts dict that becomes the manifest’s hygiene_drop_counts.
Assign validation folds. assign_validation_folds scores each sample from its measured transmission, sorts samples by score and id, and assigns each consecutive block across five folds using a seeded SHA-256 ordering. Every swatch from one sample stays in the same fold. No name-derived filament category participates.
Cross-validate and refit. Five temporary fits each train on four folds and predict the fifth, producing exactly one out-of-fold prediction per clean row. The pooled dE76/OKLab metrics drive the publication gate. After validation, a sixth fit trains on all clean rows and supplies the published parameter vector. als_fit provides an alternating-least-squares warm start, then joint_polish refines with scipy.optimize.least_squares.

fit_camera_transform returns a frozen CameraTransformFitResult carrying the final params, the cleaned frame, out-of-fold predictions, the sample-to-fold assignment, validation/final-fit metrics, and hygiene counts. The parameter layout, feature map, and monotone-curve construction are the model form — see The Camera Transform and lib.camera_transform.
The LUT bake — numeric inverse on a grid
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.lut is one function. bake_inverse_lut samples a grid_size = 33 cube over [0,1]³ appearance space, calls invert_forward from lib.camera_transform to solve back to transmission at each grid point, clips to [0,1], and returns a (33, 33, 33, 3) float32 array. This is the baked G — the numeric inverse of the fitted forward model — that the generator interpolates at solve time. Why the inverse must be baked numerically rather than solved in closed form belongs to The Camera Transform.
Staged export and coordinated publication
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.export writes complete generation directories so a reader never sees half-written files. write_camera_transform_artifact validates the payload and LUT before creating a generation, then:

Writes camera_transform.json, inverse_lut_33.npz, and manifest.json into a unique temporary generation, computes the two data-file hashes into the manifest, and fsyncs all three files.
Renames that temporary directory to gen-<timestamp>-<uuid> through _rename_generation_with_retry, making the staged generation complete but not necessarily current. On Windows only, access-denied and sharing/lock violations (winerror 5, 32, or 33) are retried after bounded delays of 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00, and 2.00 seconds. Other errors fail immediately; exhausting the retries fails without advancing CURRENT.
If activate=True, activate_camera_transform_generation writes and atomically replaces CURRENT, then finalize_camera_transform_generation removes legacy flat files and attempts to garbage-collect old generations with keep=1. This direct activation mode remains available, but production fitting uses activate=False. Cleanup is best-effort: an old generation that Windows still has locked can remain as an unregistered filesystem orphan, but it is not retained as a selectable or current Calibration fit.

Any failure before the generation rename removes the unfinished temporary directory and re-raises, so a failed staged build leaves CURRENT untouched. The production publication wrapper also discards a complete staged generation if activation or SQLite registration raises. build_payload is the sibling that stamps the schema, model version, architecture string, and parameter layout into the JSON.
Production activation is owned by publish_camera_transform_fit. It advances CURRENT, then registers a replaceable SQLite camera_transform fit whose artifact root is the Camera Transform family directory and whose artifacts are the newly hashed CURRENT pointer plus the three files in the selected generation. Registering the pointer is essential: publication readiness verifies both the pointer hash and the generation it names. Only after SQLite replacement succeeds does the wrapper finalize keep-1 garbage collection. If activation fails, it discards the staged generation. If an ordinary SQLite publication exception occurs, it restores the previous pointer and discards the staged generation. This is a coordinated pointer/database replacement with compensation, not one cross-filesystem/SQLite transaction.
A process kill is outside that compensation. If Calibration stops after CURRENT advances but before SQLite replacement commits, pointer-reading consumers can load the new generation while model status still names the old fit. No startup publication journal completes or reverses this transition. Publication readiness detects the registered-pointer/hash mismatch rather than repairing it. Do not kill Calibration while Fit Models is publishing; after an abnormal stop, verify model status and readiness before trusting or publishing the working set.
The fingerprint — what actually reached the optimizer
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.fingerprint answers “does this need rebuilding?” more robustly than a sample count. build_camera_transform_fit_fingerprint re-runs load_and_filter and assign_validation_folds, then hashes the rows that reach validation/final fitting plus the deterministic fold assignment. It produces fit_input_hash, raw_corpus_hash, validation_hash, and diagnostic_hash under CT_FINGERPRINT_SCHEMA_VERSION = 3, with floats canonicalized to 17 significant digits. The fit policy records five-fold validation followed by a final all-data fit; it contains no filament-name classification metadata. The job stores the whole fingerprint as the manifest’s source_data_fingerprint; robust_fit_input_hash reads it back for rebuild decisions.
Parity — a migration oracle, not steady state
calibration.fitting.camera_transform.parity is read-only and transitional. It captures a legacy (or stored) corpus plus hygiene and validation-fold assignment into a deterministic snapshot, so the parity oracle can prove the extraction-path switch preserves membership, row order, skips, folds, and per-row values. It is a verification harness invoked from tests/tooling, not part of the live build path.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.title: The extraction pipeline
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.content:
In one sentence: process_sample turns an oriented strip photo and registered blank into per-swatch display colors and linear transmission, builds a pending-review ExtractionResult, and—on committed SQLite runs—publishes that result, sample state, and the source/strip visuals as one recoverable unit; extract_strip_manual supplies the four-corner fallback when automatic location is unsuitable.

This page maps the production code path from evidence to a stored extraction. For the physical meaning of flatfield division and transmission, see Extraction. For the operator workflow, see Processing and extraction and Assigning images.
Related: calibration.processing.processor · calibration.processing.extraction · calibration.processing.manual · calibration.processing.extraction_result · calibration.processing.artifact_sinks · calibration.processing.extraction_visuals · calibration.processing.blank_registry · Extraction artifact sinks and blank registration
Live entry points and execution modes
The stateless image math lives in processing/extraction.py. Production orchestration belongs to three callers:

process_sample in processing/processor.py is the automatic path used by single-sample processing, the retained backend batch/reprocess helpers, thumbnail regeneration, and automatic maintenance re-extraction.
extract_strip_manual in processing/manual.py replaces automatic strip location with four operator-selected corners while reusing the shared flatfield, boundary, measurement, result, and publication contracts.
maintenance_reextract.py runs noncommitting automatic/manual extraction into a candidate workspace and applies an accepted candidate through the extraction-publication coordinator.

commit=True may change the durable sample and extraction result. commit=False never changes either one, but its visual destination depends on the caller: thumbnail regeneration intentionally recreates live derived source/strip JPEGs, ordinary manual preview writes a transient review directory, and maintenance writes a candidate directory.
The browser’s Process All does not invoke processing.processor.process_batch; it loops over the single-sample route. The retained Python batch function and /api/process/batch route are still callable backend paths, but are not the current Processing Queue UI path.
Stage 0 — geometry and sampling configuration
SwatchConfig carries num_swatches, border_mm, step_w_mm, step_h_mm, physical lightbox dimensions, open_side, and sample_fraction (default 0.50). __post_init__ derives total strip dimensions and border fractions. _build_swatch_config projects the sample’s stored strip definition through SwatchConfig.from_experiment, falling back to dataclass defaults for missing legacy geometry fields. The measurements are only meaningful when these values match the printed strip; see Geometry and strip definition.
Stage 1 — preview detection and full-resolution measurement
Automatic extraction is deliberately two-resolution:

load_preview_jpeg extracts a RAW embedded thumbnail (or reads a raster), applies the image’s stored rotation, and caps the longest dimension at 2000 px. If no preview can be decoded, the processor falls back to the full visual render.
After location succeeds, load_raw_both returns an 8-bit visual BGR render and a linear float32 RGB render. RAW input uses camera white balance for both; the linear decode uses gamma=(1,1), disables auto-brightening, and normalizes 16-bit output to [0,1]. Raster input is normalized/linearized and converted to the same visual-BGR/linear-RGB contract.

The processor applies the stored strip-image rotation and the sample’s open-side rotation to the source preview and full arrays. It independently applies the blank’s stored rotation, then uses match_flatfield_orientation to align the blank’s lightbox orientation with the source frame.
Stage 2 — automatic strip location
find_strip_contour first finds and slightly insets the lightbox region; if no lightbox is found, it searches the full frame. It tries these strategies in order and returns the first acceptable hull:

flatfield per-channel ratio deviation;
flatfield absolute difference;
Otsu BINARY_INV;
Otsu BINARY;
Canny edges;
LAB chroma and then HSV saturation; and
a geometry-sized synthetic rectangle when the lightbox itself was found.

Each image strategy tries individual convex hulls and then a merged-fragment hull. Candidate scoring rejects implausible area fractions and aspect ratios relative to the configured strip/lightbox geometry. Because strategy 7 can synthesize a contour, failure means all image strategies failed and no lightbox rectangle was available.
On a committing contour failure, the processor saves processing_status="failed", deletes any prior extraction result, and removes live sample visuals. A noncommitting run only returns the failure. Other pre-commit pipeline exceptions follow the same commit-versus-preview distinction.
Stage 3 — deskew and direction
deskew_strip uses cv2.minAreaRect, rotates the frame, crops the strip with DESKEW_PAD_PX = 6, and forces a landscape result. deskew_strip_linear applies the same transform to a second array so the visual and linear domains remain pixel-aligned.
The preview contour is used for cheap early rendering. After the full image is loaded, the processor runs contour detection again at full resolution. If that fails, it scales the preview contour into the full frame and records provenance that does not pretend it was a full-frame detection.
Automatic extraction compares the left and right fifths of the deskewed strip and rotates it 180 degrees when the brighter, nominally thinner end is on the right. Manual extraction deliberately does not use this brightness heuristic; its corner order and recorded open-side orientation are authoritative.
The processor records a spine score in its diagnostics. An optional gut-check can convert a nonpositive score into low_confidence/flagged, but _SPINE_GUT_CHECK_ENABLED is false by default, so the current normal runtime records the score without automatically flagging on it.
Stage 4 — register and divide the blank
The full linear blank is rotated into the source frame. register_flatfield detects the lightbox border in blank and source and warps the blank with a homography. If either lightbox or the homography cannot be found, the automatic path logs a warning and resizes the unregistered flatfield to the source dimensions.
register_flatfield_strict, used by the manual path, performs the same homography but raises FlatfieldRegistrationError instead of using that resize fallback. This is a physically-correct-or-fail boundary for operator-selected extraction.
Automatic extraction then deskews the registered blank with the same source contour and applies the same left/right flip. Manual extraction first registers the blank in the full source frame, perspective-warps source/linear/blank through the same clicked quad, and rotates all three together.
apply_flatfield calculates:
transmission = clip(strip_linear / max(registered_blank, 1e-6), 0, 1)
Stage 5 — swatch extent, boxes, and measurements
detect_swatch_extent derives the active swatch rectangle from physical strip geometry and the measured pixel scale. Automatic deskew passes the 6 px padding; edge-to-edge manual perspective output passes zero. The bottom is inset to 95% of step_h to avoid the open-edge over-extrusion region.
find_swatch_boundaries currently returns pure equal spacing across the known active width. It still calculates a column gradient, but the signal-snapping branch is unreachable below the early return and is not part of current behavior.
swatch_sampling_boxes_from_boundaries shrinks each cell to its configured central sampling fraction. Those half-open boxes are shared by the median sampler and the transmission-ROI overlay, so a review overlay represents the pixels the current code sampled.
For each swatch:

median_color_bgr takes the per-channel median of the visual BGR patch and returns display RGB/hex; and
the processor takes the per-channel median of the flatfield-corrected linear RGB patch and rounds R_linear, G_linear, and B_linear to six decimals.

The registered blank’s median over the active region is retained as I0_linear. The per-swatch values, I0_linear, and source/blank filenames form the compatibility Measurements object that feeds the canonical result builder.
Manual four-corner extraction
The manual endpoint receives corners in the rotation-baked preview frame in tl,tr,br,bl order. The server derives the preview-to-raw scale with the stored source rotation accounted for. extract_strip_manual:

scales the corners into the rotated full-image coordinate space;
loads and applies stored rotations to source and blank;
strictly registers the blank lightbox to the source frame;
perspective-warps the visual source, linear source, and registered blank through the same quad;
applies the open-side rotation to all three;
performs the shared flatfield division, geometric boundaries, boxes, and medians; and
either returns a preview or commits through the shared result/publication path.

Ordinary commit:false manual extraction writes all review artifacts to a transient maintenance/manual_extraction_reviews/{sample_id} directory. Its UI Accept action re-runs the extraction with commit:true; it does not promote the preview files or preview measurements directly.
Building and committing the canonical extraction result
build_extraction_result projects the new Measurements into an ExtractionResult with a fresh ext_<uuid> ID, sample/geometry identity, automatic or manual method, provenance, evidence binding, diagnostics, every swatch (including fit-excluded swatches), and review_state="pending_review".
Appearance is the builder’s intentional impure step. It calls the Camera Transform corpus’s embedded-JPEG extraction helper using the caller-resolved source and sampling geometry. Success fills each swatch’s appearance bucket and decode diagnostics. Failure records diagnostics.appearance_error, leaves appearance absent, and does not fail the transmission extraction.
commit_extraction_result sets the replacement sample state (processed or optional flagged), measurements, flag reason, and review_accepted=False. On SQLite it calls save_extraction_result_with_sample, which saves the replacement result and sample workflow state in one database transaction. The JSON compatibility backend uses a sidecar snapshot/save/sample-save/restore fallback.
If build or save fails, the function clears the attempted in-memory outputs and re-raises without saving a new failed sample. SQLite rolls its transaction back; JSON restores the prior sidecar snapshot. The processor catches this specific aborted commit and reports a rolled-back failure, leaving the prior durable sample/result pair authoritative. This differs from a normal detection/pipeline failure, which deliberately persists failed and removes an old result.
Commit is not review acceptance. A successful new result remains pending review until the operator’s later Accept action atomically synchronizes the sample flag and the sidecar’s review state. Only current accepted extraction results are eligible fitting evidence.
Recoverable SQLite visual publication
Committed SQLite automatic/manual extraction does not write directly to the observable thumbnail paths. It creates a hidden StagedLiveThumbnailSink and writes only the durable live pair, source.jpg and strip.jpg. Before the semantic callback runs, publish_extraction_update copies and fsyncs both JPEGs into a durable publication directory and writes a journal containing prior/replacement extraction IDs and origin metadata.
After SQLite makes the replacement ID current, the coordinator promotes both visuals with rollback-capable sibling replacements. If ordinary visual promotion fails, the operation reports pending recovery rather than undoing already-committed semantics. Startup compares each journal with the current extraction-result ID: it discards uncommitted/superseded work, republishes the current pair, completes origin-specific bookkeeping where safe, and preserves ambiguous/invalid records for diagnosis. resolve_visual_path prefers a unique current journal payload while recovery is pending.
This gives process-kill convergence across the database/filesystem boundary without pretending they share one atomic transaction. See Extraction artifact sinks and blank registration for directory names and recovery details.
Blank registration
On SQLite, /api/blanks/register relates an existing managed image_assets row to a new registered_blanks row. It does not copy the image. The CSV importer can create pending blank relations and all associated sample assignments in one combined SQLite transaction.
The JSON compatibility path instead copies the source into blanks/{blank_id}{suffix}, records best-effort EXIF time, and deletes the copy if registration fails. For the current rotation/invalidation limitation affecting images used as blanks, see Extraction artifact sinks and blank registration.
Backfill is migration, not extraction
processing/backfill.py is a one-shot compatibility migration for legacy samples that already contain Sample.measurements but lack a canonical extraction result. It classifies records and builds sidecars only for the eligible class. It does not re-run transmission extraction and does not mutate legacy measurements. It is not imported into the steady-state processing path.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.title: The maintenance backend
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/t.content:
In one sentence: every standard maintenance chore is one frozen MaintenanceOperation in calibration.maintenance’s single OPERATIONS registry, run through a uniform preflight → execute → JSON report lifecycle whose report carries a structured frontend-refresh impact; the heaviest operation, Re-extract Sample Images, is registered as preflight-only and uses a separate staged backend (calibration.maintenance_reextract) that builds a candidate set the operator reviews sample-by-sample before anything overwrites accepted data.

This page maps the framework: how an operation is defined and registered, the lifecycle that runs it, the refresh impact it reports, and the staged re-extraction candidate store. It deliberately does not explain what each operation means or when to run it — for that, see Maintenance Operations (the mechanism, per operation) and Running maintenance (the operator surface). The one-operation-at-a-time run lock lives in the server, not here (see Web API and job orchestration); the Fit Models operation delegates to the model workflow (Model workflow, publication, and review); and re-extraction commits write through the stores in Data access and persistence.
Related: calibration.maintenance · calibration.maintenance_reextract · Maintenance Operations · Running maintenance · Web API and job orchestration
An operation is a frozen dataclass in one registry
MaintenanceOperation is a frozen dataclass — the whole definition of one chore. Its fields:

Identity and display — operation_id, name, category (e.g. "Audit", "Images", "System Maintenance", "Geometry Artifacts", "Calibration Models"), description.
Risk and modes — risk_class (e.g. "read_only", "cleanup", "writes_derived_files", "writes_user_output", "changes_semantic_data"), a tuple of allowed modes and a default_mode, and a writes flag.
Concurrency metadata — resource_claims describes everything the operation reads or writes (for example "sqlite_semantic_state", "preview_cache", and "geometry_artifacts"). conflict_resources is the smaller, enforced set of ordinary-writer categories that must remain stable while the operation is queued or running. Both are exposed by public_dict; the server uses the latter at its shared maintenance resource gate.
Cancellation metadata — cancellation_policy is either "safe_points" or "not_supported"; the derived cancellable boolean is exposed to the frontend. Public job state also includes dynamic cancel_available, which becomes false after a cancellation request is accepted or the job reaches a terminal state.
Availability — enabled plus an unavailable_reason string for operations that are registered but not runnable.
Behavior — two Callable[..., dict] | None callables, preflight and execute.

public_dict serializes everything except the two callables — that dict is what the API hands the frontend. All operations live in one module-level OPERATIONS: dict[str, MaintenanceOperation]; list_operations returns their public dicts and get_operation looks one up by id (raising KeyError on an unknown id). The registry spans audits, image/artifact rebuilds, a read-only SQLite integrity check, geometry export, model fitting, and re-extraction.
The two resource lists intentionally differ. A filesystem audit may read SQLite to discover ownership without needing to freeze every unrelated database-backed edit, while an integrity operation can require a stable database snapshot by declaring the enforced sqlite_write conflict. Image custody/preview, extraction evidence/sample visuals, geometry state, and model evidence/artifacts have their own conflict categories. Ordinary browsing remains available, except that source and blank preview GET routes acquire a preview_cache writer lease when they may generate a missing JPEG on demand.
The preflight → execute → report lifecycle
Two module functions drive every operation uniformly:

preflight_operation resolves the mode (defaulting to default_mode), rejects a mode not in operation.modes with ValueError, and short-circuits a disabled operation into a synthetic blocked result carrying its unavailable_reason. Otherwise it calls operation.preflight(store, mode, scope). Preflight is read-only: it computes the target set and blockers so the operator can confirm before writes happen.
execute_operation re-validates mode and enablement, then introspects the execute function’s signature with inspect.signature and passes through only the optional kwargs it accepts — preflight, confirmation, job_id — alongside the always-present progress_cb and should_cancel. This is how one caller drives execute functions with different signatures. After the operation returns its report dict, it writes it to disk via report_path_for + _atomic_write_json and stamps report_path onto the returned payload.

Reports are canonical JSON. _report builds the "prisma-maintenance-report-v1" schema: operation_id, mode, scope, status, timestamps, a summary dict, findings, changed_paths, blocked, warnings, errors, and the ui_refresh impact. Findings are built by _finding with a severity/category/target/message shape and tallied by _count_findings. Reports land in reports_dir(store) = <app-managed-root>/output/maintenance/reports/, named {timestamp}_{operation_id}_{job_id[:12]}.json; the same maintenance root holds a .tmp scratch dir (temp_dir) and a quarantine dir (quarantine_dir). startup_scan_interrupted_temp lists leftover temp entries from an interrupted run so _run_post_store_startup_checks can report them to the console at boot.
Quarantine Orphaned Artifacts has a deliberately narrow destructive boundary. It can move only direct preview JPEGs whose exact filenames are not expected by a current image/blank record, strictly named interrupted publication files directly inside a sample-thumbnail directory, direct sample-thumbnail directories with no matching sample, direct managed geometry-artifact directories with no matching geometry, and 64-hex fingerprint directories that are direct children of a live geometry but are not its recomputed current fingerprint. Preview ownership is computed once after the operation has reserved preview_cache; this avoids re-listing every image and blank for every orphan while keeping ownership stable through the run. Geometry fingerprints and live-row ownership are still revalidated per target, so a fingerprint that becomes current is skipped. Source photographs, blank source files, SQLite, models, backups, RAW archives, public geometry exports, and reports are not eligible. Quarantine is only a seven-day filesystem safety buffer: prune_quarantine_runs deletes expired Prisma-named runs during startup/activity housekeeping, while malformed entries and anything containing a filesystem link are skipped and reported.
Source preview cache stems come from a SHA-256 digest of stable image_asset_id (source_preview_cache_stem in processing/extraction.py), with the rotation suffix added afterward. The filename fallback exists for the legacy backend. Consequently, same-stem files with different extensions and filenames containing cache-like __rN text cannot share a SQLite source-preview key. Older filename-derived JPEGs have no current owner: the missing-preview audit requests regeneration under the current key and the orphan audit can quarantine the old cache files.
Preview publication is pair-safe against ordinary in-process exceptions. generate_preview_jpeg encodes and verifies both same-directory staged JPEGs before publish_staged_files replaces either live file. The publisher copies existing targets to rollback siblings, promotes with os.replace, and restores already-promoted targets if a later promotion raises; a rollback failure preserves and reports its recovery copy. Rebuild Extraction Images Only similarly stages all requested source.jpg/strip.jpg replacements for one sample and promotes that sample’s set together. Cancellation or one renderer failure before/during the guarded call removes or rolls back the staged set.
That multi-file helper has no process-kill journal. A hard stop between two os.replace calls can leave one live JPEG new and its sibling old, with stage/rollback files beside them. Startup does not choose a recovery copy or restore the pair; the orphan/quarantine tools can identify or move the strictly named leftovers but do not repair the mixed live set. Re-run the appropriate rebuild after an abnormal stop and verify the previews/visuals before discarding recovery files.
Progress and cancellation are cooperative only for operations registered with the "safe_points" policy: execute functions call _progress to emit phase/current/total updates and _cancelled to poll the should_cancel check, returning a status of "cancelled" when interrupted. The job API changes accepted requests to "cancelling", preserves its resource reservation, and reports terminal cancellation only after the executor returns. Repeated requests while cancelling are idempotent; unsupported and terminal requests receive HTTP 409 from cancel_maintenance_job. Audit Library Integrity, SQLite Integrity Check, and Fit Models are registered as "not_supported" and run to completion once started.
"safe_points" means stop between operation-defined units, not generic rollback. Work completed before the safe point remains completed: already-moved quarantine targets stay quarantined, already-published preview or sample-visual units stay published, and already-written geometry outputs remain. The preview and sample-visual publishers protect each current unit with staging/rollback, but the framework does not reverse earlier units when a later cancellation is observed.
The frontend-refresh impact
Every operation report describes what the UI must invalidate after it runs. The vocabulary is fixed by ui_refresh_none, the canonical empty impact:

a kind of "none", "targeted", or "full";
four coarse booleans — reload_app_data, reload_import_data, rerender_workspace, rerender_open_drawers;
four fine-grained invalidation sets — invalidate_preview_cache (by filename / blank id), invalidate_sample_thumbnails (by sample id / kind), invalidate_geometry_artifacts (by geometry id), and invalidate_model_artifacts (by filament id / model type), each with an all flag; plus a display message.

An audit reports ui_refresh_none — it changed nothing. A write operation reports a targeted impact naming what it touched: for example _execute_rebuild_image_previews includes reload_import_data, rerender_workspace, rerender_open_drawers, and the rebuilt filenames/blank ids in invalidate_preview_cache. merge_ui_refresh combines impacts when an operation aggregates sub-steps — booleans OR together, the list-valued invalidation sets union (deduped by _merge_unique), and kind escalates toward full.
The current frontend consumes this impact automatically only in the standard job’s succeeded branch in showMaintenanceWorkflow/applyMaintenanceRefreshImpact. A safely cancelled write report may therefore describe completed partial changes without automatically refreshing the rest of the open application; a manual Refresh Data reconciles that display. This is a frontend follow-up, not a stronger rollback guarantee from the backend.
Two operations that delegate outward
Most operations implement their own preflight/execute in maintenance.py. Two hand off:

Fit Models (refit_calibration_models) is the maintenance entry to the whole calibration-model pipeline. Its executor _execute_refit_calibration_models converts scope to options with options_from_scope and calls execute_model_fit_workflow (from calibration.fitting.model_fit_workflow), then wraps that workflow’s status, findings, partial-publication metadata, and ui_refresh into a maintenance report. The physics and publication of that fit belong to Model workflow, publication, and review.
Re-extract Sample Images is registered with only _preflight_reextract_sample_images_operation and no execute. Its multi-phase preflight/generate/review/apply lifecycle is handled by dedicated job registries and routes in the server rather than the single-shot execute contract (see Web API and job orchestration).

Staged re-extraction — a non-destructive candidate store
calibration.maintenance_reextract (maintenance_reextract.py, “Staged candidate storage and sample-image re-extraction workflows”) re-runs image extraction for already-accepted samples without touching live data until the operator explicitly commits. The whole design is a stage-then-review-then-apply cycle keyed on a candidate set.
Scope options
_normalize_scope defines three independent scope axes, and _mode_supported is the gate on their combinations:

domain_mode — "complete", "transmission_only", or "appearance_only": which parts of the extraction result get regenerated.
segmentation_mode — "existing_coordinates" (replay extraction at the sample’s stored swatch coordinates) or "redetect_from_scratch" (re-run detection; only valid with complete).
sample_scope — {"kind": "all_accepted"} or {"kind": "sample_ids", ...} for an explicit list.

The candidate store
Staged artifacts live under reextract_root(store) = <store.root>/maintenance/reextract_sample_images/, one directory per id-validated rext_<32 hex> candidate set. create_candidate_set writes a ReextractManifest containing schema version, scope (workflow_options), plan_digest, per-status counts, sample ids, and generation/apply report ids. Each ReextractCandidatePayload records its status, source/blank fingerprints, the current extraction_result_id it was staged against, the replacement result when applicable, and staged source/blank/strip/transmission/appearance JPEGs. Statuses include ready_changed, ready_unchanged, manual_required, failed, blocked, stale, applied, and rejected_in_candidate_set. Creating a new set prunes older sets; prune_candidate_sets retains at most the explicitly preserved set or, during ordinary housekeeping, the newest recoverable set no older than seven days, and removes other validly named sets. Candidate paths and cleanup use root-confined path validation and safe recursive deletion; link-like candidate entries are skipped or refused.
Generation is a family of functions: preflight_reextract_sample_images plans the target rows and blockers; generate_reextract_candidates is the main producer; generate_appearance_existing_coordinate_candidates is the appearance-only path; generate_manual_candidate handles operator-guided re-detection; retry_candidate re-runs one member of a non-appearance set. The current UI exposes Retry for failed or stale candidates, although the backend helper itself does not enforce that status restriction; appearance-only retry is not implemented and requires a fresh set.
Generation cancellation never commits accepted extraction data. It leaves the candidate-set manifest as cancelled/incomplete and retains whatever staged candidates were completed so the set can be inspected, retried, or discarded. Candidate images are written before the final candidate JSON; a cancellation or hard stop in that narrow interval can therefore leave an incomplete staged row, or on Retry/Manual Corners leave older candidate metadata beside newly written staged images. That inconsistency is confined to the candidate store, not the accepted corpus.
Per-sample save/skip review
A candidate carries a separate ReextractReviewPayload holding the operator’s decision — one of pending, save, skip (STAGED_REVIEW_DECISIONS). update_candidate_review sets one sample’s decision and rejects changes to a non-ready candidate; update_candidate_reviews_bulk changes ready candidates and counts non-ready rows as skipped. A candidate with nothing to change still has ready status and defaults to pending; a non-ready one defaults to skip (_default_review_decision). Apply is blocked until manual or incomplete rows are resolved, every ready candidate is explicitly Save or Skip, and at least one is marked Save (_saved_sample_ids_from_reviews).
Non-destructive commit — save vs discard
apply_reextract_candidates is the only step that writes to live accepted data, and it is deliberately paranoid:

Appearance-only sets delegate to apply_appearance_candidates; both paths require the SQLite backend.
It applies only the sample ids the operator marked save (_saved_sample_ids_from_reviews); ready candidates marked Skip are counted and left untouched.
The complete/transmission path re-verifies staleness before writing — the current accepted extraction still exists and its extraction_result_id still matches what the candidate was staged against, the source/blank files still match (_candidate_sources_still_match), and the stored semantic digest is unchanged. Any mismatch flips the candidate to stale and skips it rather than overwriting drifted data.
Only a surviving ready_changed candidate’s semantic callback calls store.replace_accepted_extraction_result, which swaps the accepted extraction and returns the dependent model fits it just marked stale (stale_model_fit_ids); a ready_unchanged candidate keeps the same extraction id and republishes the live source/strip visuals.
Appearance-only apply checks that the accepted extraction id and source-image identity still match, then calls SQLiteDataStore.update_extraction_result_appearance. It does not currently compare the staged old_appearance_digest before writing. The store distinguishes any persisted metadata change from model_inputs_changed, so decoder-version metadata alone does not alter Camera Transform’s corpus or stale the current fit; such a result is counted as applied_unchanged.

Complete/transmission publication is process-kill recoverable per sample. publish_extraction_update in processing.extraction_publication journals the semantic and visual publication unit, and complete_reextract_publication makes candidate/review state converge after the live extraction is committed. Startup calls reconcile_publications before candidate pruning and defers pruning when recovery is ambiguous. Appearance-only apply does not use this publication journal: its SQLite update and later candidate-status write are separate operations, so a hard stop between them can leave live appearance data newer than the staged candidate metadata. A clean completed apply deletes its candidate set; partial, cancelled, or failed sets remain for review or another apply (_finalize_apply_report).
Cancellation is checked between samples and immediately before the short non-interruptible per-sample publication unit. Samples already published stay applied; unprocessed saved candidates remain staged, and the manifest/report records cancellation so apply can be run again. The dedicated frontend reloads the candidate-set review after a cancelled apply but currently performs the full application refresh only after succeeded, so other open Calibration surfaces can require Refresh Data to reflect already-applied samples.
Because staging, review, and apply are separate steps, an operator can generate a whole set, inspect each sample, and discard it entirely with delete_candidate_set — the accepted corpus is never modified unless apply runs and a candidate clears every freshness check. The commit itself flows through the SQLite store (see Data access and persistence); the run lock that keeps only one standard maintenance or dedicated re-extraction job in flight at a time is held in the server (Web API and job orchestration).

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Assigning images
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: on Images → Assign Images, a three-pane workspace connects the raw lightbox photos you shot outside the app to your samples — you import the photos, register the empty-lightbox blanks that flatfield correction needs, then give each sample a strip image, matching blank, and open-side orientation so it is ready to extract.

Extraction can’t run until a sample knows three things: which photo is its printed strip, which photo is the empty-lightbox reference, and which way the strip’s open side faces in the photo. This screen is where you supply all three. A blank is a photograph of the lit lightbox with no strip on it; during extraction the strip photo is divided by the blank to cancel the lightbox’s spatial unevenness — that division is the flatfield correction. See Extraction for how the blank is actually used.
Reach this screen from the Images tab, Assign Images subtab. The three panes read left to right: Registered Blanks, Image Inbox, and Assign Images and Blanks.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Processing and extraction · Samples and geometries · Extraction

The three panes
Image Inbox (center)
This is where raw photos enter the app and where you pick the one to assign.

Import from Inbox verifies and copies supported files placed directly in the user-facing Inbox into managed custody. After the SQLite commit, custody finalization removes a successfully imported source from the Inbox; exact duplicates are moved under Removed Images. Nothing else on this screen can use a new photo until it has been imported.
Open Inbox Folder opens the exact user-facing Inbox folder used by this running app, so a user does not have to guess which installation receives a file.
Clean Up Unused moves eligible managed images into the user-facing Inbox/Removed Images tree and deletes their custody rows. It leaves assigned strip images and blanks referenced by samples alone.
CSV Bulk Assignment opens the bulk-assignment dialog (below).

The grid groups thumbnails into collapsible Unassigned, Assigned, and Ignored sections. An available unassigned image has both a rotate button (Rotate thumbnail 90 degrees clockwise) and an ignore button (the ×). An assigned image retains the rotate button but cannot be ignored until it is unassigned. An ignored image instead has a restore button and cannot be rotated. Ignore is persistent UI state; it does not move or delete the managed file.
Rotation is stored as a per-image 90-degree override. The server clears stale preview-cache variants, and extraction reads the override for both detection and measurement. A strip image cannot be rotated while it belongs to a processed, failed, or flagged sample. For a still-editable assignment, rotating the strip image clears its open-side orientation and returns an assigned sample to unassigned, so the user must confirm the orientation again.
There is an important current asymmetry for registered blanks: the same rotation override is used when the blank is read, but changing a blank’s rotation does not automatically find or invalidate samples that already use that blank. Set a blank’s rotation before processing samples with it. If it must change later, reprocess the affected samples before fitting models.
Below the grid, Selected Image names the thumbnail you’ve clicked, with two footer actions:

← Register as Blank turns the selected photo into a flatfield reference (it moves to the Registered Blanks pane).
Assign Image to Sample → attaches the selected photo to the sample selected in the right pane as its strip image.

Registered Blanks (left)
The catalog of empty-lightbox references. To add one, either select a photo in the inbox and click ← Register as Blank, or drag a thumbnail onto this pane’s drop zone (Drop image to register blank, shown compactly as Drop to Register). Registration assigns an id and records capture time from EXIF when available. SQLite reuses the managed image asset and inserts the registered_blanks relation; only the legacy JSON path copies a second file into blank storage.
Selected Blank names the blank you’ve clicked; Assign Blank to Sample → attaches it to the sample selected in the right pane.
Register one blank per capture session and reuse it across samples shot without changing the lightbox, camera/lens position, exposure, or other capture conditions. It does not have to correspond to a particular printed strip, but it must represent the same imaging setup.
Assign Images and Blanks (right)
The sample list shows what each sample has so far. Selecting a row here sets the target for the two → assign buttons in the other panes; Selected Sample echoes your choice. Each sample’s assigned image and blank appear as slots with an Unassign (×) control to detach either one. The four-arrow control records whether the strip’s open side points up, right, down, or left.
The sample enters Ready For Processing only when all three inputs are present and locally available: strip image, registered blank, and orientation. Changing or clearing the image or blank, or changing the stored orientation, invalidates earlier processing for that sample — the app clears stale results so the sample re-extracts against the current evidence rather than showing measurements from the old inputs.
The current UI lets a user click the active orientation arrow as though to clear it, but that null value is omitted from the request: the card appears pending only until the next data refresh, while the server retains the old orientation and still considers the sample ready. Until that frontend/backend defect is fixed, select the correct replacement direction directly; unassigning the strip image is the reliable way to clear its orientation.

The assignment loop
For one sample by hand:

Import from Inbox to bring your session’s photos in.
Register the session’s empty-lightbox shot: select it, ← Register as Blank (do this once per session).
Select a sample in the right pane.
Select its strip photo in the inbox, Assign Image to Sample →.
Select the session blank in the left pane, Assign Blank to Sample →.
Use the arrows on the sample card to say which way the strip’s open side faces.

Repeat 3–6 for each sample. When every intended sample appears under Ready For Processing, move to Processing and extraction.

Import progress, cancellation, and interruption
Import from Inbox starts a background job and opens a progress dialog. The dialog polls the in-memory job record every 500 ms, retries transient status failures, and cannot be closed while the import is active. A second start request joins the already-active import rather than starting a competing one. Image import is also excluded while backup, restore, RAW archive work, another import, or conflicting maintenance holds the relevant resources.
Before it changes persistent state, the importer scans and hashes every supported file in the Inbox. If any file fails that scan, the batch reports the errors and imports none of them. During the write phase it creates a durable custody journal, copies each new image into managed storage, verifies the copy’s hash, and inserts the new custody rows in one SQLite transaction. An exact filename-and-content duplicate is skipped and moved under Removed Images when the transaction is finalized.
Cancel is cooperative. If it reaches a cancellation check before the SQLite commit, the transaction rolls back, newly created managed copies are removed, and the Inbox sources remain available. Once the database commit has completed, the import must finish custody finalization; a late cancel is reported as a successful import that completed before cancellation took effect.
The progress job itself exists only in memory and cannot be resumed after a server restart. The custody transaction is durable, however: startup/next-import reconciliation removes uncommitted managed copies or completes the Inbox cleanup for a committed import. This converges persistent image custody even though the old progress dialog and job id do not survive.
Clean Up Unused is different. It is a confirmed, synchronous request with a busy state, but no progress job or cancel control. It handles eligible images one at a time, moving each managed file before deleting its SQLite custody row. Normal failures are reported per image and later images continue. Do not kill the server during cleanup: a hard stop between a file move and its row deletion can leave a custody row whose managed file is missing, and retry currently skips rather than repairs that row.

CSV Bulk Assignment (the bulk path)
For many samples at once, CSV Bulk Assignment assigns images and blanks from a spreadsheet instead of clicking each one. Place every referenced sample and blank image in the Calibration Inbox first, click Import from Inbox, and then open the bulk dialog. The flow is template → validate → commit.
Download CSV Template gives you a header-only file with four columns:

























ColumnWhat goes in itSample IDThe sample’s id (exp-123), or just the number 123 when that number is unambiguous.Sample ImageThe imported strip photo’s filename (extension optional) or managed image id. Use a name/id, not a filesystem path.Blank ImageA registered blank’s id, or an imported photo filename/id — an unregistered photo here is registered as a blank during commit. Use a name/id, not a filesystem path.OrientationWhich way the strip’s open side faces: U, D, L, or R (T is accepted as up, B as down).
Choose CSV loads your filled-in UTF-8 file; Validate CSV checks it without changing anything and returns a preview: a per-row table plus counts of rows ready, blocked, blanks to register, and warnings. Extra columns are ignored with a warning. A row is blocked (and skipped) when its sample or image can’t be found, an image is ambiguous, a photo is missing or ignored, an image is already assigned to another sample, the same sample/image is reused elsewhere in the CSV, the sample photo is also the blank, or the sample isn’t eligible.
CSV assignment only touches fresh samples: a row is rejected if the sample already has an image, a blank, an orientation, a non-unassigned status, or existing extraction results. This makes bulk import a safe first-fill, not a way to overwrite work you’ve already done.
The validation preview and its commit token live only in server memory, expire after 15 minutes, and disappear on restart. Commit rechecks the live samples, images, assignments, and blanks; if anything relevant changed after validation, it rejects the stale preview instead of applying an outdated plan.
The commit button reads Import Assignments when every row is clean, or Import Valid Rows when some are blocked (only the ready rows commit). If any ready row names a photo that isn’t a registered blank yet, you’re asked to confirm registering those blanks before the import proceeds. Blank registration and all ready sample assignments then commit as one SQLite transaction: a failure leaves neither partial assignments nor a newly registered-but-unused blank. On success the app reports how many assignments landed and how many blanks it registered. CSV validation and commit are synchronous requests; they do not expose progress or cancellation.
