prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Backup and restore
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the topbar Backup / Restore dialog creates a portable ZIP of either the SQLite library alone or the library plus its durable files, validates and previews a package before restoring it, and separately archives bulky camera-RAW files so they can be removed from and later returned to active storage.

This page covers making backups and restoring them, plus the raw-image archive workflow that lives in the same dialog. It is a manual, operator-initiated screen; the app also keeps its own automatic database snapshots behind the scenes (see Automatic restore points below), which are a different thing and are not managed here.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Running maintenance · Managing filaments

Opening the dialog
The topbar Backup / Restore button opens a single dialog titled Backup / Restore with four stacked panels: Create Backup, Restore From Backup, Archive RAW Images, and Restore Archived Images. Everything below maps to one of those panels.
Backup creation, library restore, RAW-archive creation, archived-image removal, and archived-image restore all use the same custody lock, so only one can run at a time. Inbox import, model publication, and internal SQLite restore-point application also coordinate through that lock. A running Maintenance job blocks the operations on this screen, and library restore or archived-image removal also refuses to start while a model fit that could conflict with it is active. A rejected start normally reports Backup or restore is already running or names the active blocker.
These jobs have progress displays but no user-cancel action. Closing the dialog does not stop the server-side work. Let a job finish, especially a restore or archived-image removal; the Interruption and restart behavior section explains what happens if the server process itself stops.

Create Backup
Under Create Backup, pick a backup type, then click Create Backup. Two choices:
Essential Data Only
A small package containing a consistent SQLite snapshot — filaments, geometries, samples, image assignments, extracted measurements, model-fit records, and the rest of the database state. The private snapshot keeps only the lifecycle-owned fit for each model family; it does not modify the live database while doing so. The package does not contain source images, model artifact files, or generated STEP/STL exports.
Restoring it replaces only SQLite and leaves the current files and exports in place. That makes it a quick, portable snapshot of the workbook’s knowledge, not a self-contained library: files left beside an independently restored database are not guaranteed to match its records.
All Data and Artifacts
The operational working state: the normalized SQLite snapshot plus durable files from Calibration’s managed asset tree and supported .step/.stl geometry exports. This includes accepted sample visuals such as source.jpg and strip.jpg and the durable model artifacts needed by the retained fits. It deliberately omits regenerable preview-cache JPEGs, interrupted thumbnail transaction files, manual-review images, staged re-extraction candidate sets, generator cache files, logs, lock files, and other temporary work. Those are not restore invariants and their absence does not make backup creation fail.
When All Data and Artifacts is selected, an Include raw image files checkbox appears. Leave it on to include recognized camera-RAW originals (.cr2, .cr3, .dng, .nef, .arw, .raf, .rw2, and .orf). Turn it off to keep the database, non-RAW managed files, extracted data, durable artifacts, and geometry exports while omitting those multi-gigabyte originals. This switch does not remove ordinary JPEG/PNG assets from the package. The checkbox only applies to All Data and Artifacts; Essential Data Only contains no asset files at all.
The backup is written as a timestamped .zip in Calibration’s visible Backups folder, and the result supplies both its path and a download action. If Windows temporarily prevents a completed, validated ZIP from being promoted out of the backup .tmp workspace, Prisma preserves it there and retries during startup or later housekeeping. Invalid or unrecoverable abandoned temporary entries are retained for a 24-hour grace period before cleanup. Move important packages somewhere safe; the Backups folder is local working storage, not an off-machine backup by itself.

Restore From Backup
Under Restore From Backup, point the Backup File control at a Prisma backup .zip (type or select its path), then click Restore Backup.
A full All Data and Artifacts backup is also the supported way to move an existing Calibration library into a fresh Suite release: create the backup in the old copy, keep the ZIP outside both Prisma folders, start the new blank copy once, and restore the ZIP through this dialog. Do not copy Calibration/Workspace by hand or point two Prisma copies at one working directory. After restore, verify the sample/image counts and Modeling status before retiring the old copy.
Restore never applies a package blind. It first validates the manifest, member paths and hashes, SQLite integrity/schema, package semantics, and required file references, then shows a preview of the package and what it can replace. Validation is synchronous, so its progress display is animated but intentionally indeterminate rather than a file-by-file percentage. The preview token expires after 15 minutes if unused; a local path is also checked again for identity and validity when the restore starts.
Only after validation does the app ask you to type the package’s exact confirmation phrase. The wording differs by package: an all-data package with RAW warns that it will replace all existing data; one without RAW says it will replace all existing data except source images; and an essential-data package says it will replace the current database. The action stays disabled until the normalized phrase matches.
Before replacing live state, the restore job creates a fresh database-only safety backup. If the strict backup cannot be made it attempts a more permissive emergency core backup; if neither succeeds, the restore aborts before applying the package. The subsequent restore progress is six coarse phases, with package validation/staging shown as indeterminate rather than byte-counted.
What a restore replaces depends on which package you are restoring:

Essential Data Only → replaces the database only; your current images and exports stay as they are.
All Data and Artifacts, with raw images → replaces the database, assets, and exports, and brings in the package’s raw images too.
All Data and Artifacts, without raw images → replaces the database, assets, and exports, but keeps your current raw source images in place (the package has none to supply).

When restore finishes, the app reconstructs the active SQLite store and refreshes the UI automatically. Restore refuses unsafe symlinks, junctions, and reparse points at its managed boundaries; a linked managed asset tree is rejected before replacement, while a later unsafe-path failure is handled by the rollback transaction. This prevents a disposable worktree link from silently redirecting destructive work into another library.
During replacement, Prisma writes a durable restore journal and moves displaced state into a restore_previous_* rollback directory. The new workspace becomes authoritative only after validation, a store smoke check, and a durable committed journal phase. An ordinary failure before commit rolls the old state back. After commit, cleanup removes the rollback workspace; if that cleanup fails, the restore remains successful and reports restore_previous_cleanup_failed with the residual path so it can be removed manually after the restored library is verified.

Archive RAW Images
Raw camera files are the largest thing in the library and, once extracted, are rarely needed day to day. The Archive RAW Images panel lets you move them out of the active library without losing them. It has two steps, deliberately separated so you never delete originals you have not safely stored first.
Create RAW Image Archive
Create RAW Image Archive packages the current recognized camera-RAW image assets into a standalone archive ZIP. It records file identity and library-use context and validates the completed package. It only copies — nothing is deleted or moved out of the active library. Missing RAW files are recorded as missing and reported as a warning rather than silently represented as archived. Do this first, verify the archive, and move it somewhere safe.
Remove Archived Images From Active Library
This is the destructive step. Point its Archive or Backup File control at the archive you just made (a RAW-image archive, or an All Data and Artifacts backup that includes RAW files), and the app validates it and reconciles the package against the current SQLite image catalog. Because it deletes local files, it is confirmation-gated: type Remove archived images from active library before the action enables.
For every candidate, Prisma rechecks the archive entry, managed relative path, SQLite hash/size identity, and actual local file hash/size before a root-confined delete. Images absent from the package, changed since archiving, or otherwise conflicting are skipped and reported; they are not silently deleted. Store the archive somewhere safe before running this step.

Restore Archived Images
Restore Archived Images is the inverse: select a RAW-image archive ZIP (or an all-data backup that includes RAW files) and click Restore Archived Images. The app validates and reconciles it, then restores only files that are missing, represented in the current SQLite catalog, and still match the catalog’s expected identity. It uses exclusive creation and final hash/size verification, so an existing matching file is left alone and an existing conflict is not overwritten. Afterward it attempts to regenerate affected source thumbnails and reports samples whose extraction visuals still need a Maintenance rebuild.
Interruption and restart behavior
The operations on this screen are noncancelable. Closing a workflow window merely hides it; killing the server terminates its in-memory job and progress record.

Backup or archive creation: an incomplete, unvalidated temporary ZIP is disposable and housekeeping removes it. A complete validated ZIP that failed only during final promotion is retained for automatic recovery.
Library restore: this is the process-kill-safe workflow. On the next startup, the durable journal rolls back every noncommitted restore or finishes cleanup for one that had already committed. If Prisma cannot prove which files are safe to keep or remove, startup stops in recovery mode instead of guessing.
Archived-image restore or removal: work is committed one image at a time and has no full-operation rollback journal. If the process stops, files already restored or removed remain that way. Reopen the workflow, validate the archive again, and retry; reconciliation skips completed matches and reports conflicts. Avoid intentionally killing the server during removal because the final file’s custody-state update can lag its deletion until a retry reconciles it.


Automatic restore points (not this dialog)
Separately from this dialog, Calibration maintains internal SQLite restore points. Startup considers creating a database-only snapshot, with a six-hour minimum interval, and prunes the collection to at most 12 points no older than 30 days. They contain no RAW images, managed artifacts, or ZIP package. Applying one first preserves the displaced SQLite files under output/restore-points/recovery/; those preservation runs are not selectable restore points and are pruned with the same default count/age bounds.
Restore points are an automatic corruption-recovery safety net, not portable user backups and not something managed in this dialog. See Data access and persistence for the persistence and recovery boundaries.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Driving the calibration app
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the calibration app is a single-user FastAPI logbook that walks a filament from a printed strip to a published Generator library — register filaments and geometries, create samples, assign lightbox photos, extract and accept per-swatch measurements, curate the evidence, fit Calibration’s working models, and explicitly publish a static copy — while scoped resource guards keep conflicting writers from overlapping.

This page serves two readers: the operator driving the app end to end, and the developer who needs the backend’s shape — how the app is wired, which backend stores the data, and why a second job returns a “busy” error. For the phenomena behind each step (what a measurement is, how the models work) see the How It Works section; for the code-level map see the Technical Reference.
Related: Managing filaments · Samples and geometries · Assigning images · Processing and extraction · The Modeling page · Maintenance operations

Starting the packaged app
The Windows Suite starts this server through Prisma Calibration.exe; the Linux Suite uses the executable Prisma Calibration (Prisma/calibration_launcher.py). Both enter the same launcher. It fixes the app root to the folder containing the executable, creates and probes Calibration’s portable folders, takes an exclusive lock on Calibration/Workspace, creates a blank SQLite database only when that workspace is genuinely blank, applies the SQLite/database/asset environment contract, reserves a loopback port (preferring 8016 and trying the next 19 ports), and asks the host platform to open the browser. Starting a second instance for the same healthy workspace opens the lock owner’s local URL instead of creating a second writer.
server.py builds one FastAPI instance titled Unified Calibration Workbook and, after defining the API routes, mounts the single-page frontend from calibration/app/ with html=True, so / resolves to index.html. All operational routes live under /api/...; everything else is the static frontend. index.html loads the native-module entrypoint bootstrap.js, which composes the endpoint modules in api/, shared services in core/, and workflow owners in features/; style.css preserves the ordered stylesheet cascade. See Frontend architecture.
Starting from source
Use the same launcher rather than importing server.py directly. From the repository root, synchronize both runtime groups and create a separate runtime root so personal data does not land inside the source checkout.
On Windows PowerShell:
uv sync --frozen --only-group generator-runtime --only-group calibration-runtime --no-install-project
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$HOME\PrismaRuntime"
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m Prisma.calibration_launcher --app-root "$HOME\PrismaRuntime"
On Linux or macOS:
uv sync --frozen --only-group generator-runtime --only-group calibration-runtime --no-install-project
mkdir -p "$HOME/PrismaRuntime"
.venv/bin/python -m Prisma.calibration_launcher --app-root "$HOME/PrismaRuntime"
The source launcher and blank SQLite initialization have been health-smoked under Ubuntu 24.04/WSL2 as well as Windows. The POSIX lock and macOS browser-opening paths have been statically audited, but Prisma has not been run on a Mac and macOS support is not currently claimed. Direct server.py execution remains a lower-level developer interface: it requires explicit backend configuration plus the matching SQLite or JSON paths and does not establish the complete portable runtime contract for you.
Which store the data lives in
The backend is chosen explicitly at launch and never falls back silently. server.py reads PRISMA_CALIBRATION_BACKEND and accepts only json or sqlite. The packaged/source launcher always supplies SQLite, Calibration/Workspace/calibration.sqlite3, Calibration/Workspace/Assets, and the portable app root through the runtime-layout environment contract. The older JSON file store and local pointer-file compatibility remain explicitly selectable for migration tools, tests, and source maintenance; they are not packaged-runtime fallbacks.

The workflow, end to end
The five top-level tabs are workspaces, not a left-to-right wizard: the visible order is Logbook, Images, Filaments, Geometries, and Modeling, while the usual dependency order starts by setting up the reusable Filaments and Geometries libraries. You then create samples in Logbook, assign/process their images, and curate/fit in Modeling.
1 — Register the building blocks
Before a sample can exist, its parts must be in the library:

Filaments tab → + New Filament opens the create drawer: color name, manufacturer, material, hex color, and the policy checkboxes (White-cap eligible, Special role: Transparent, Special role: Black, and Exclude from model fits). The exclusion also withholds that filament from newly published libraries. See Managing filaments.
Geometries tab → + New Sample Geometry opens the step builder, where you lay out the strip’s variable and fixed layers. Related geometries can be grouped with Manage Bundles. See Samples and geometries.

2 — Create samples
A sample is a strip geometry filled with specific filaments. On the Logbook tab, + New Samples opens the bulk create drawer: pick a single geometry or a bundle, assign a filament to each layer role (in Multi mode you batch across several filaments to spawn many samples at once), and create. The sample now exists in the logbook awaiting photographs. See Samples and geometries.
3 — Assign photographs
The physical strips are 3D-printed and photographed on a lightbox outside the app. On Images → Assign Images, a three-pane workspace connects those raw photos to samples:

Image Inbox — Open Inbox Folder opens the user-facing drop folder; Import from Inbox moves supported files into managed custody. Import is the action that scans the folder; the topbar Refresh Data button does not import it. Select an imported image and use Assign Image to Sample →.
Registered Blanks — a blank is an empty-lightbox photo used for flatfield correction. Register one, then Assign Blank to Sample →.
Assign Images and Blanks — the sample list showing what each sample has so far.

For many samples at once, CSV Bulk Assignment bulk-assigns images and blanks from a spreadsheet. See Assigning images.
4 — Extract the colors
On Images → Processing Queue, samples with images assigned appear under Ready to Process. Process All (N) runs strip detection, deskew, flatfield correction, and per-swatch color extraction across the batch. Samples that fail auto-detection land in Failed or Flagged for Manual Processing, where Manual Process opens a modal to click the strip’s four corners by hand. See Processing and extraction.
5 — Accept the results
Extraction results appear in Post-Processing Review (the right side of the Processing Queue). You Accept or Reject each result. Accepting promotes it to the sample’s trusted extraction; rejecting does not make it model evidence. Only accepted extractions feed the models and appear in Modeling’s evidence tables.
6 — Curate the evidence
The Modeling tab is where you decide what the models learn. Overview summarizes accepted evidence and flags stale/missing models, samples blocked by excluded filaments, and samples without an accepted extraction. Samples lists accepted-extraction samples and exposes persistent sample/swatch inclusion controls through the comparison drawer; Filaments shows accepted-evidence coverage and health. Excluding a sample or swatch keeps a suspect measurement out of later fits without deleting it. See The Modeling page.
7 — Fit the working models
Fit Models opens the dedicated, noncancelable Maintenance workflow. It always attempts Color Model v1 (the legacy spline) and Color Model v2 (the photo-stack model) from the currently included evidence. Camera Transform preflight rebuilds that family only when forced or when its registered inputs/artifacts are missing, invalid, or changed; it is skipped when already current and can also be skipped when fewer than five eligible samples exist. Each successful stage coordinates its own filesystem/pointer and SQLite replacement and compensates for ordinary exceptions, but neither that cross-layer transition nor the multi-family workflow is one process-kill-safe transaction. A completed family—or v1’s successful filament subset—can already be current before a later failure stops the run. Generator cannot see this mutable working state. The mechanics live in Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform.
8 — Publish a Generator library
The topbar Publish Models action first reads /api/models/publication/readiness, which requires one current registered fit for every required family, intact registered artifacts/pointers, and a valid public filament catalog. Publish to Generator calls /api/models/publication/install and installs a new inactive, application-immutable library in the sibling Generator store. Export Library Package calls /api/models/publication/export and writes the equivalent transfer ZIP to Calibration/Output/Published Models. Calibration will not mutate either published copy afterward. Neither path activates a Generator library, changes Calibration’s working-model lifecycle, or modifies an older published library.

How the app is wired (developer view)
One process, one user
The app holds its live state in a single Python process. There is no per-user or per-browser isolation: two tabs pointed at the same server share one backend and one set of jobs. This is a workbench tool, not a multi-tenant service.
Conflicts are scoped, not global
Calibration does not have one global heavy-job lock. It combines operation-family job registries with explicit resource ownership:

the backup/restore/RAW-custody lock serializes package and image-custody work;
the model-fit owner prevents conflicting fit/evidence writers;
the extraction-writer owner protects accepted extraction evidence and sample visuals;
Maintenance reserves the concrete resources declared by an operation before its worker starts.

Independent reads and nonconflicting work can overlap. Conflicting work is rejected with HTTP 409 and a blocker message. Depending on the endpoint, a repeated same-operation start may instead return the already-active job. Nothing waits in a general-purpose queue for an unrelated heavy operation to finish.
The practical UI pattern is start, poll, report. A click starts or joins the relevant background job, the frontend polls its operation-specific status route, and only workflows classified for safe cancellation expose a Cancel action. Other workflows are intentionally noncancelable; see Web API and job orchestration, Running maintenance, and Backup and restore for the individual contracts.
Restarting
Restarting the server drops the in-memory job registries, so a browser cannot resume polling an old job id. Durable state lives in SQLite and the managed asset/output roots: accepted extractions, filaments, geometries, samples, normally completed working models, staged re-extraction review sets, backups, and published Generator libraries survive independently of the worker that created them.
That does not mean every interrupted operation is rolled back wholesale. Startup reconciles the workflows that have durable journals or housekeeping rules — notably full restore, image import custody, complete/transmission extraction publication, backup temporary-package promotion, and immutable-library staging cleanup. It does not reconcile a hard stop between a working model’s filesystem/pointer activation and SQLite replacement. Other workflows retain only their completed units or staging data. If the process stops during work, restart through the launcher and inspect the affected workflow rather than assuming the old progress panel remains authoritative; after an interrupted fit, use Publish Models readiness as the stricter artifact-integrity check.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Managing filaments
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the Filaments tab is the library of every filament Calibration knows about — you add each one once, giving it a name, manufacturer, material, and color, and set policy metadata that controls white-cap classification, special roles, and model-fit exclusion.

A filament must exist in this library before any sample can reference it. This page covers adding a filament and reading or changing its policy; the layer-by-layer strip that filaments get poured into lives on the Samples and geometries page.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Samples and geometries · The Modeling page · Color Model v1 · Color Model v2 · The Camera Transform

The Filaments table
The Filaments tab is a sortable table, one row per filament, with a summary line above it (e.g. “N filaments, M profiled”). Columns:

Filament — the color name, with its color chip.
Manufacturer.
ID — the slug (see below).
Samples — how many samples reference this filament.
Processed — how many of those have extracted measurements.
Profile — whether a fitted spline profile exists for it.

The toolbar has one button, + New Filament, which opens the create drawer. Clicking any row opens that filament’s view drawer.

Adding a filament
+ New Filament opens a drawer headed New Filament with a Create button. Fill in:

Filament — the color name, placeholder e.g. Basic Cyan.
Manufacturer — placeholder e.g. Bambu. As you type, previously-used manufacturers autocomplete from the library.
Material — placeholder e.g. PLA; defaults to unknown.
Hex Color — a color picker swatch and a hex text field, kept in sync. Must be #RRGGBB.
The Policy checkboxes and Notes (below).

A Generated ID field previews the slug live as you type the manufacturer and color name. The slug is {manufacturer}-{color_name}, lowercased, with every run of non-alphanumeric characters collapsed to a single hyphen — so “Bambu” + “Basic Cyan” becomes bambu-basic-cyan. If that ID already exists in the library the drawer warns you and blocks the save; manufacturer, color name, and a valid hex are all required. The ID is permanent once created — there is no rename.

The policy checkboxes
Four checkboxes under Policy set how the rest of the system may use this filament. They are the load-bearing part of this screen.
White-cap eligible
Marks the filament as a candidate for the white cap — the diffusing white layer a lithophane is printed against. Calibration snapshots every filament with this flag into the model-white classifier used by the legacy spline and photo-stack fits. A published model library carries the same classifier into Generator, where the configured white base and cap must belong to it. Turn the flag on for white and near-white diffusers; leave it off for colored filaments.
Changing this flag makes affected current legacy-spline and photo-stack fits stale. It does not stale the camera transform, whose corpus does not use the white/color classification.
Special role: Transparent / Special role: Black
Two independent tags that record a filament’s special optical role — a fully clear/transparent filament, or a true black. They are stored on the filament record as descriptive metadata; a filament can carry either, both, or neither. They do not exclude the filament from anything on their own — that is what the exclude flag below does.
Exclude from model fits
The consequential one, and the reason it is styled as a warning. The checkbox itself is labeled Exclude from model fits. When checked, Calibration drops any sample that references the filament from all three production fit families: Color Model v1 (the legacy spline), Color Model v2 (the photo-stack model), and The Camera Transform. Changing the flag also makes affected current fits stale.
There is a related publication effect, but it is not a second live connection between the apps. A model library published after the change records exclude_from_model: true and generation_available: false for that filament. Generator then refuses to use it in new model-backed generation work. An already published library is a static snapshot and does not change when Calibration’s live filament record changes.
Two things are worth being precise about:

It drops the sample, not just the swatch. Exclusion is evaluated per sample. A sample is removed from a fit whenever the excluded filament appears in it in any role — whether it is the variable filament being characterized or one of the fixed backing layers underneath. One excluded backing filament therefore quietly removes every sample printed on top of it from the evidence.
It is a standing filament policy. This is not a per-run toggle. It is distinct from the per-sample and per-swatch fit controls on The Modeling page, and remains in effect until you uncheck it.

Use it for a filament you have retired, mis-measured, or never intend to print with — it keeps that filament’s data from polluting the models without your having to delete it or hunt down every sample by hand.

Notes and read-only fields

Notes — a free-text textarea for anything you want to remember about the filament.
Used By N Samples — read-only; lists the samples that reference this filament (click through to open them).
ID — read-only; the slug, shown for reference.


Viewing and editing
Clicking a row opens the view drawer: name and chip, manufacturer, material, color (hex and RGB), a Policy summary (White Cap, Special Roles, Model Fit, Generation), notes, the used-by list, and the ID.
Edit (top of the view drawer) switches the same drawer into edit mode, exposing the fields and policy checkboxes with three buttons:

Save — commits the changes and returns to the view.
Discard — abandons the edits.
Delete — removes the filament, but only if nothing depends on it. A filament that is referenced by any sample, has a saved profile, or has processed strip data cannot be deleted; the app tells you so rather than deleting. Retiring such a filament is what Exclude from model fits is for.

Editing lets you change the manufacturer, color name, material, hex, policy flags, and notes. It does not change the ID — the slug is fixed at creation.

Color note: the Hex Color you set here is a display-referred label for the UI, not a measurement. The actual optical behavior of the filament comes from its extracted samples, in a different color domain entirely — see Transmission vs Appearance.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Processing and extraction
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: on Images → Processing Queue, run extraction for samples whose strip image, registered blank, and open-side orientation are ready; rescue automatic failures with the four-corner manual workflow; then Accept only the results that should become model-fitting evidence.

This is the operator’s reference for the Processing Queue screen. The image math—detection, deskew, flatfield division, and per-swatch median extraction—is covered in Extraction and The extraction pipeline. Assignment and evidence readiness are covered in Assigning images.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Assigning images · Extraction · The extraction pipeline · The Modeling page
Getting here and what counts as ready
Open Images and switch from Assign Images to Processing Queue. The screen is split into Pre-Processing Queue on the left and Post-Processing Review on the right.
A normal ready sample has all of the following:

an assigned strip image whose managed file is locally available;
an assigned registered blank whose managed file is locally available; and
a selected open-side orientation.

The durable workflow status must be assigned for the sample to appear under Ready to Process. Merely assigning an image and blank without an orientation is not sufficient. If a managed source or blank later becomes unavailable, the card can still reflect its stored workflow state, but the processing request fails with a specific unavailable-file error rather than fabricating a result.
Pre-Processing Queue
The left pane has three collapsible sections.
Ready to Process
Each ready card shows its strip layout and assigned evidence, with these actions:

Process sends one synchronous request for this sample.
Flag moves it to Flagged for Manual Processing without extracting it.
Reassign unassigns the strip image, clears any flag best-effort, and returns the sample to Assign Images.

Process All (N) takes a snapshot of the currently assigned sample IDs and processes them sequentially in the browser. It does not call the backend’s /api/process/batch route and it is not one persistent server job. For each sample, the frontend calls the same single-sample endpoint used by Process, waits for its response, refreshes application data, updates the processed/flagged/failed counters, and only then begins the next sample.
The progress panel is therefore determinate between completed samples, not within the extraction of the current sample. There is no Process All cancel control. Closing or reloading the page prevents the browser loop from starting later samples, but it does not cancel the synchronous request already running on the server. Samples committed before interruption remain committed; Process All progress itself is not persisted or resumed after relaunch.
Failed
A committing automatic extraction normally marks the sample failed, removes its extraction result, and removes its live sample visuals when detection fails or another pipeline exception occurs before a successful commit. This prevents an earlier result from masquerading as the output of the failed attempt.
There is one deliberate rollback distinction: if building or atomically saving the replacement extraction result/sample pair fails, commit_extraction_result restores the prior durable pair and re-raises. The processor reports that attempt as failed without saving a new failed state. A filesystem publication interruption after SQLite commits is handled differently again: the committed semantics remain authoritative and the journal converges source.jpg and strip.jpg at startup. See Extraction artifact sinks and blank registration.
Flagged for Manual Processing
A user can explicitly Flag a sample. The backend also retains an optional low-spine-confidence path, but its gut-check is disabled by default in the current runtime, so ordinary automatic extraction does not normally create low-confidence flags.
Cards in Failed and Flagged for Manual Processing have:

Manual Process to open the four-corner workflow;
Unflag to clear the flag; a failed sample returns to assigned only if its image, blank, and orientation are complete, while a flagged sample with an extraction result returns to processed; and
Reassign to detach the strip image and return to assignment.

Manual Process All (N) opens the same modal with a client-side queue. It advances only after the operator accepts each manual result; it is not a server-side batch job.
Concurrency and busy behavior
Each automatic single-sample request and each ordinary manual preview/commit request acquires the extraction writer guard. That guard conflicts with model fitting and with other operations that reserve the same extraction/SQLite/evidence resources. A conflicting request receives a busy response; it is not silently queued.
Because the UI’s Process All releases the guard after every single-sample request, it does not reserve the extraction resource for the whole batch. Another client or operation can acquire a conflicting resource between items. The local UI disables its own overlapping processing controls while its batch state is active, but the backend remains the authority for cross-window and cross-operation admission.
Ordinary manual processing
Manual Process and Manual Process All open Manual Processing. The canvas uses the rotation-baked source preview. Click the corners in this order:

top-left;
top-right;
bottom-right;
bottom-left.

Placed corners can be dragged. The normal controls are:

Extract & Process sends a synchronous commit:false request. It writes transient review images and shows the extracted strip, but does not change the durable sample or extraction result.
Reset Corners clears the selection.
Retry discards the displayed result and returns to corner placement.
Accept re-runs the same manual extraction with commit:true; it does not merely promote the preview. A successful commit creates a new pending-review extraction, clears the flag through the committed workflow state, and advances the client-side manual queue or closes the modal.

The ordinary manual request has no cancel control. While it is running, close/reset controls are disabled and the browser waits for the synchronous response. Closing or killing the client cannot cooperatively cancel the in-flight server call. The Cancel button present in the shared modal is shown only when the modal is being reused for a cancellable maintenance re-extraction candidate job; it is not part of ordinary Processing Queue manual extraction.
Manual preview artifacts live under maintenance/manual_extraction_reviews/{sample_id}. Retry only hides the current result; the next preview overwrites that workspace. Closing, committing, or failing requests its removal, and startup removes abandoned manual-review directories. A hard stop during preview does not commit sample semantics. A hard stop during commit follows the same extraction-publication recovery rules as automatic extraction.
The manual path treats the clicked corner order plus stored open-side orientation as authoritative and does not use the automatic path’s brightness-based left/right flip. It strictly registers the blank to the source lightbox and fails if that homography cannot be established; it does not fall back to an unregistered resize.
Post-Processing Review
A successful automatic or manually committed extraction is already durable when it appears in Post-Processing Review. Its ExtractionResult.review_state is pending_review, and the sample’s review_accepted flag is false. The card shows the source and blank, the extracted strip, a thickness row, and a mock strip derived from the measured display colors.

Accept does not run extraction again. It atomically sets the SQLite sample’s review_accepted=true and synchronizes the current extraction result to review_state="accepted". Accepted results are the extraction evidence eligible for model fitting.
Reject invalidates the current extraction result, clears its measurements and flag, removes derived visuals, marks affected model fits stale as required, and returns the sample to assigned when its evidence is still complete (otherwise unassigned).

Accept All and Reject All apply those actions sequentially to the cards currently in review, refresh from the backend, and report partial failures.
There is a current single-card Accept error-path defect: if the backend update fails, the frontend logs the error but still hides the card locally until Refresh Data restores the authoritative state. Bulk Accept does not have that particular behavior; it collects and reports failed updates. This is a tracked implementation finding, not intended persistence semantics.
Acceptance is separate from later fit controls. On the Modeling tab, an accepted sample, swatch, or filament can still be excluded from fitting without rejecting or deleting the underlying extraction.
Safe interruption summary









































WorkflowExecution modelCooperative cancel?Restart/process-kill boundaryProcessOne synchronous server requestNoCurrent request may finish without the browser; committed SQLite/visual publication converges from its journal on restart.Process AllBrowser loop of synchronous single requestsNoCompleted samples persist; current request follows single-process behavior; later items are not started and progress is not resumed.Manual previewOne synchronous commit:false requestNoNo durable extraction mutation; abandoned review files are removed at startup.Manual AcceptOne synchronous commit:true re-runNoSemantic/visual publication uses the same recover-forward journal as automatic extraction.Maintenance manual candidateBackground re-extraction job with pollingYes, at safe pointsCandidate-workspace rules apply; this is not the ordinary Processing Queue workflow.
Short version

Finish image, blank, and open-side assignment.
Use Process All or Process and let the current request finish.
Manually process failures by clicking TL, TR, BR, BL, previewing, then committing with Accept.
In Post-Processing Review, accept trustworthy results and reject bad ones.
Continue to The Modeling page; only accepted current extraction results are fitting evidence.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Running maintenance
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the topbar Maintenance button opens a dialog of named housekeeping operations — audits, image and geometry rebuilds, database health checks, and the model fit — each of which you run through the same preflight → run → report cadence, one at a time, with a running Maintenance Activity Log; the one exception is Re-extract Sample Images, a staged review workflow that never overwrites your accepted data until you explicitly save.

This page is the operator’s how-to for the Maintenance dialog: what each control does and in what order you click it. For what each operation does mechanically — what an audit inspects, what a rebuild regenerates, why the fit is safe to re-run — see Maintenance Operations and don’t re-derive it here.
Related: Maintenance Operations · Processing and extraction · The Modeling page · Backup and restore · Driving the calibration app

Opening the dialog
The topbar Maintenance button opens the Maintenance dialog. Operations are laid out as selectable cards, grouped under category caps and spread across up to three columns. Each card shows the operation’s name, a one-line description, and a small meta tag telling you whether it is Read-only or writes something. Clicking a card selects it; the Selected Operation panel on the right then shows a Start Workflow button.
The dialog header carries one extra button, Activity Log, covered below.
The operations, by group
The groupings and exact names come straight from the operation registry:

Audit — Audit Library Integrity, Audit Missing Artifacts, Audit Orphaned Artifacts, Audit Source Image Custody. All read-only; they report problems without changing anything.
Images — Rebuild Image Previews, Rebuild Extraction Images Only, Re-extract Sample Images.
Calibration Models — Fit Models.
Geometry Artifacts — Regenerate STEPs/STLs, Export Geometry Files.
System Maintenance — SQLite Integrity Check, Quarantine Orphaned Artifacts.

An operation that is currently unavailable appears grayed out with a reason line in its detail panel, and its Start Workflow button is disabled.
Two of these overlap actions you can reach elsewhere:

Fit Models here runs the exact same unified fit you can launch from The Modeling page — Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and the Camera Transform, from the currently-included evidence.
Export Geometry Files writes the same user-facing STEP/STL exports that the Geometries tab’s export action produces.


Running a standard operation
Every operation except Re-extract Sample Images runs through one workflow dialog with the same three beats.

Start Workflow opens the operation’s dialog, headed with the operation name. It restates the description and, where relevant, exposes options:

Operations with more than one mode show a Mode picker — for the rebuilds and exports this is Missing Only (act only on what’s absent or repairable) versus Force Rebuild / Force Export (rewrite everything in scope). A help line explains the difference.
Export Geometry Files adds an Export Options block: Only Geometries Used By Samples or All Geometries, plus STEP / STL file-type checkboxes.
Fit Models adds a Fit Options block with a Force Camera Transform checkbox.


Run Preflight inspects the current state and reports what the operation would do — a summary, any warnings, and any blockers — without touching data. If preflight blocks the operation, the run button stays disabled.
The run button (labeled by what it does: Run Audit, Run Maintenance, Export Files, or Fit Models) executes the job. Progress streams into the dialog. Safe-point operations offer Cancel and remain visibly Cancelling… until the worker actually stops; operations labeled Runs to completion never offer Cancel. A Result section then shows the outcome, summary, any warnings, and the path to the saved report. Export Geometry Files in its overwrite mode also asks you to type a confirmation phrase before the run button unlocks.

That preflight-first-then-run rhythm is deliberate: nothing that writes data does so until you have seen the preflight and clicked the run button.
Only one at a time
Maintenance operations are not queued. Only one standard maintenance worker or dedicated re-extraction worker may execute at any moment. A second standard start is normally rejected with 409 and a message naming the active job; family/resource admission rejects conflicting re-extraction starts as well. There is one race-safe qualification: a request can create a queued record just before its daemon worker acquires the shared run lock. If another owner wins, that record is marked failed/blocked rather than waiting or running concurrently. Backup, restore, or RAW-archive work blocks maintenance in the same way, and vice versa — see Backup and restore. In practice you start a job, watch it finish in its dialog, and only then start the next.

The Activity Log
The Activity Log button (dialog header) opens Maintenance Activity Log, a history of standard-operation reports. It is a four-column table: Name, Type, Status, File Name. Each standard executor that returns its structured report gets one report row here; the newest sits on top. A job blocked before execution—or a worker that raises before returning a report—has no row. The dedicated Re-extract Sample Images workflow keeps its generation/apply reports inside its candidate set rather than adding them to this list. A clean completed re-extraction apply deletes that candidate set, so its candidate-local reports are not a durable Activity Log history.
The footer’s Clear Log button deletes those saved report files. It asks first (a Clear Activity Log confirmation), and it is narrow in scope: clearing the log removes only the maintenance report JSON files — it does not touch backups, RAW archives, source images, generated artifacts, quarantine files, SQLite data, or any sample records.

Re-extract Sample Images
Re-extract Sample Images is not a one-shot job — it is a staged review workflow, and the important thing to understand is that it is non-destructive: it re-runs extraction into a temporary candidate set and leaves your accepted measurements untouched until you explicitly save. You review every candidate and decide, sample by sample, whether to keep it.
Start Workflow on this card opens its own dialog with three scope controls:

Data — Complete, Transmission Only, or Appearance Only. This chooses which color data gets recomputed. (See Transmission vs Appearance for what those two halves are.)
Coordinates — Use Accepted Coordinates (reuse the strip corners already accepted for each sample) or Re-detect Strip (find the strip from scratch). Choosing Re-detect Strip forces Data back to Complete and disables the partial options — a full re-detect has to redo everything.
Samples — All Accepted (every accepted, processed sample) or Selected Samples, which reveals an id textarea. Type or paste sample ids separated by commas or spaces, e.g. exp-055, exp-056.

From there:

Run Preflight counts the targets and splits them into automated, manual, and blocked, and warns you which samples will need manual corners.
Extract Images runs the re-extraction into a fresh candidate set. Nothing accepted has changed yet.
Samples that couldn’t auto-detect surface in a manual step first: open each one, place Manual Corners by hand, then Review Results.
The Review Extracted Images dialog lists every candidate with a before/after strip comparison (Extracted Transmission and Extracted Appearance). For each reviewable sample, toggle Save or Skip; a failed candidate offers Retry, and a re-detect candidate offers Manual Corners. You must decide Save or Skip on every pending sample before you can commit.
Commit with Save Results (which shows the final Save / Skip / Failed / Blocked counts) or throw the whole candidate set away with Discard Results. Only Save Results writes the kept candidates over the accepted measurements.

Like the standard operations, each active re-extraction phase takes the shared maintenance run lock. A second re-extraction or standard maintenance job cannot run concurrently; admission normally rejects the conflicting start, while a queue-to-worker race is recorded as blocked rather than waiting.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Samples and geometries
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the Geometries tab is where you design the printable strip shapes — variable and fixed layer roles, exported as STEP/STL for the printer — and group them into bundles; the Logbook tab is where you fill a geometry with real filaments to create the samples you will later photograph and measure.

This page covers two screens and the drawers they open. A sample geometry is a strip design: which layers it has and how thick each swatch is, with the material left unspecified. A sample is that geometry filled with specific filaments — one per layer role. A bundle is a named group of related geometries printed together, with their shared filament slots mapped once so you can create many samples in a single pass. For the anatomy and math behind a geometry — the staircase, the spine, the structural fingerprint — see Sample Geometry; this page stays on what you click and why.
Related: Sample Geometry · Driving the calibration app · Assigning images · Managing filaments

The Geometries tab
The table lists every sample geometry in the library, one row each, with columns Strip (a mini strip diagram), Alias, Bundle, # Layers, Used by (how many samples reference it), and Last modified. The summary above the table reads N sample geometries. The toolbar has three buttons:

+ New Sample Geometry — opens the step builder drawer to design a new strip.
Manage Bundles — opens the bundle management drawer (toggles: click again to close).
Export Geometry Files — opens the geometry-library maintenance workflow for writing user-facing STEP/STL files into the public output folder. It starts with All Geometries selected, but you can switch to Only Geometries Used By Samples, choose STEP and/or STL, and run Missing Only or confirmed Force Export (see Managed artifacts vs. exports).

Clicking a row opens its detail drawer. The drawer header carries Export and Edit; the body shows the geometry’s Alias, ID, Bundle chips, Last Modified, a Used By sample list, and the Exported Files and Managed Artifacts sections. Each stored file path has a Copy Path button that copies the absolute path to the clipboard.

Edit switches the alias field into edit mode, where the header shows Save, Discard, and Delete. A geometry’s shape is immutable once created (Sample Geometry). Bundle membership is managed independently by the Bundle chips and picker in the same drawer; adding or removing a bundle takes effect immediately rather than waiting for the alias Save action. The current drawer does not expose geometry notes. Delete opens the Delete Sample Geometry confirmation; deletion is refused if any sample or bundle still references the geometry.
Export (drawer header) opens the geometry export dialog for that one geometry.


Building a geometry (the step builder drawer)
+ New Sample Geometry opens the New Sample Geometry drawer. Its header has two commit buttons: Create (save the geometry into the library) and Create + Export (save, then immediately open the export dialog).
You lay out the strip as a stack of layer role cards, ordered bottom to top:

Each card is either Variable or Fixed. Exactly one role must be Variable — its per-swatch thickness values are typed into the swatch input grid, and this is the staircase that sweeps the thickness axis. A Fixed role takes a single thickness that applies across the whole strip.
Drag a card by its handle to reorder the stack.
+ Add Layer Role appends a new fixed role; the small remove control on a card deletes it.

The left side of the drawer is a live Visual Preview:

Top View scales the full strip footprint into the available box and reports its derived width and height.
Side View uses the same horizontal strip scale but exaggerates vertical thickness so the layer staircase remains legible.

The form on the right is divided into Strip Layout, Variable Layer Increment, Strip Definition, Strip Diagram Preview, Metadata, and Output. Variable Layer Increment is optional shorthand: enter a first swatch thickness and a swatch-to-swatch increment, then use Fill Values to populate the editable values in Strip Definition. The two previews continue to update when you edit those values directly.
The spine thickness starts at the tallest swatch stack plus 0.08 mm and continues auto-updating as the layer values change until you edit the spine field yourself. It must be at least as tall as the thickest stack. Roles are slots, not materials — the geometry never names a filament; that happens when you create samples.

Managed artifacts vs. exports
There are two distinct sets of files, and the distinction matters:

Managed artifacts are the app’s internal, canonical STEP/STL files, generated and owned by the backend and tracked against the geometry’s structural fingerprint. The drawer’s Managed Artifacts section reports how many exist.
Exports are user-facing copies written into Calibration/Output/Steps for you to hand to the slicer. The drawer’s Exported Files section records the latest export paths.

Both Create + Export and the row-level Export open the Export Sample Geometry dialog. It has a name field plus Export STEP, Export STLs, and Cancel. STEP produces one model with a labeled solid body per layer role; STLs produce one file per role, named so the slicer shows which body is which layer. If an export of the same name already exists in the output folder, a Replace Existing Export? dialog appears listing the conflicting paths, with Overwrite and Cancel. While either export request is active, the parent dialog stays open with its controls disabled; Escape, outside-click, and a second Export action cannot detach the UI from the request.
The toolbar’s Export Geometry Files button is different: it opens the multi-geometry maintenance workflow rather than exporting a single geometry. The workflow defaults to all geometries but also supports used-by-samples scope, output-type selection, missing-only generation, and confirmed force replacement.

Bundles (Manage Bundles drawer)
Manage Bundles opens the Manage Bundles drawer: a bundle list on the left, the selected bundle’s detail on the right.

Create a bundle by typing a name into the new-bundle row and clicking Create.
Select a bundle to edit it. Its header shows Rename (which reveals an inline field with Save / Cancel) and Delete.
Under Bundle Geometries, Add Geometries… adds member geometries; each member row has a remove control.
Under Bundle Filament Mapping, Edit Mapping opens the mapping editor, where you define the bundle’s shared filament slots and map each geometry’s layer roles onto them. A bundle must be fully mapped before it can drive bulk sample creation; if you save an incomplete mapping, a Save Incomplete Mapping dialog offers Save Anyway or Cancel. The bundle’s list entry shows a mapping-status pill.

A mapped bundle lets you assign a filament once per shared slot and spawn a sample for every member geometry in one action.

Creating samples (the Logbook tab)
On the Logbook tab, + New Samples opens the New Samples drawer. Its header has one commit button, Create. The drawer is a form on the left and a live Sample Preview strip diagram on the right.

Select Geometry Source — a toggle between Single Geometry and Geometry Bundle, plus a picker for choosing the specific geometry or bundle.
Selected Geometry Preview — shows the chosen strip so you can confirm it before assigning materials.
Filament slots — one row per assignable role (or per shared bundle slot). Each row has a Single / Multi toggle:

Single assigns one filament to that role.
Multi (batch) picks several filaments for one role at once; the app then spawns a separate sample for each — one strip design, many filaments under test. Only one role can be in Multi mode at a time.


Notes — an optional free-text note applied to every sample created in the batch.
Sample Summary — a running count and record preview of what Create will produce.

Because roles are just slots, one geometry serves any number of filaments — the geometry decides the shape, the sample decides the material. Newly created samples land in the logbook with no photos yet, ready for Assigning images.
A note on editing an existing sample: changing which geometry or filaments a sample uses is a provenance change. If the sample already has extraction results, the change invalidates them — the app clears the measurements and marks any dependent filament profiles stale, because the old measurement no longer describes the new material stack.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: The Modeling page
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
In one sentence: the Modeling tab is where you inspect and curate the accepted measurements available to model fitting, compare the two color models with measured swatches, and run Fit Models — which always attempts Color Model v1 and v2, replaces each successful stage, and rebuilds the Camera Transform only when its preflight says that is necessary.

This is the last stop before you can publish a complete library for Generator. Everything upstream produced measurements; this page decides which of them count, checks Calibration’s working models for staleness, and triggers the fit. It does not re-explain how each model works — for that, follow the links to Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform.
Related: Driving the calibration app · Processing and extraction · Managing filaments · Running maintenance · Color Model v1 · Color Model v2 · The Camera Transform

What “evidence” means here
Only accepted extractions appear in the Modeling sample and filament evidence tables. A sample whose processing result has not been accepted is counted under Samples without accepted extraction on Overview, but it is not a row in the Samples subtab. Accepting an extraction is done on the Processing Queue; see Processing and extraction.
Two levers coexist, and they are not the same:

Sample and swatch curation. The sample and swatch controls sideline one accepted strip or individual swatch from subsequent fits without deleting its measurement. The state persists until you include it again. These controls are available directly in the Modeling sample drawer and on the sample record in Logbook.
Persistent per-filament exclusion. The Exclude from model fits flag drops a filament wholesale from model fitting. A library published afterward records it as unavailable for new Generator work; an older published library remains unchanged. You can change the flag from Managing filaments or the filament detail drawer on this page. Use it for a retired or invalid filament; use sample/swatch exclusion for isolated suspect evidence.


The header — model status and Fit Models
The Modeling tab header carries one status entry per working model — Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and Camera Transform — plus the primary Fit Models button.

Current — Calibration has a registered fit row whose currentness_state is current; no tracked mutation has marked that row stale.
Stale — a tracked mutation to contributing evidence or another fit input has invalidated the registered working fit. A Fit Models needed banner appears above the subtabs when anything is stale or missing.
Missing — Calibration has no registered fit row for that model family.

These entries report registered currentness; they do not re-hash the model files. Publish Models performs the stricter artifact, pointer, and filament-catalog validation before it allows a library to be created.
Fit Models opens the same noncancelable maintenance workflow documented under Running maintenance and Maintenance Operations. Its preflight always schedules the legacy spline profiles (Color Model v1) and Photo Stack model (Color Model v2). The Camera Transform is scheduled only if it is forced or its registered inputs/artifacts are missing, invalid, or changed; it is skipped when current and can also be skipped when fewer than five eligible samples exist. Each published family replaces Calibration’s prior current fit, but the three-family workflow is not one all-or-nothing transaction. V1 can also publish its successful filament subset and then cause the overall workflow to fail and stop when another filament failed. It does not change Generator. Only one conflicting heavy job runs at a time, so a conflict is reported instead of starting another fit (see Driving the calibration app and Model workflow, publication, and review).
The internal publishers compensate for ordinary exceptions, but their filesystem/pointer and SQLite steps are not protected by a process-kill journal. Do not kill Calibration while model publication is in progress. After an abnormal stop, status may still reflect the registered database row while a pointer or live v1 file changed; use publication readiness as the stricter integrity check before publishing a library.
When all three status entries are current, use the separate topbar Publish Models action to validate and copy that exact set into an immutable library. Current status is necessary but not sufficient: publication can still be blocked by a missing, changed, or invalid registered artifact or by invalid public filament data. Publish to Generator installs a successful library inactive; Export Library Package writes a transferable ZIP. Generator continues using its previously selected library until you open Model Library → Manage, select the new library, and choose Activate and Restart Prisma.
Three subtabs sit under the header: Overview, Samples, and Filaments.

Overview — is the evidence healthy?
The Overview subtab is a read-at-a-glance summary. Current Evidence is a compact table:

Evidence Samples — model-eligible samples over all accepted-extraction samples (for example, 41 / 55). Eligibility requires that the sample itself is included, none of its filaments is persistently excluded, and at least one swatch remains included.
Swatches — swatches in model-eligible samples over all swatches in accepted-extraction samples.
Excluded Samples — how many samples you have toggled to Exclude.
Excluded Swatches — how many individual swatches are currently sidelined.

Needs Attention lists stale and missing models, samples blocked because one of their filaments is excluded, and samples without an accepted extraction. If none of those conditions applies it says No immediate blockers. This is a status summary, not a guarantee that every included measurement is high quality; the sample comparisons remain the place to judge that.

Samples — curate one strip at a time
The Samples subtab lists accepted-extraction samples with columns Sample, Strip, Filaments, Fit State, and Extracted Appearance. The Sample, Filaments, and Fit State headers are sortable. Above the table are two filters:

A Filter dropdown: All, Included, Excluded, Filament Excluded, Has Excluded Swatches, Stale, and Missing Model. The last two show all otherwise-matching accepted samples only while at least one model has that state; otherwise they are empty.
A filament filter: Filaments… opens a Filter Samples by Filament picker; selected filaments show as chips, and Clear removes them. Use it to see every sample that a given filament appears in.

Including and excluding a sample
Click a row to open its review drawer. The Sample Exclusion module contains Exclude Sample or Include Sample; exclusion requires a second confirming click. Excluding keeps the measurement intact but withholds the entire sample from later fits. Changing this state can mark models that used the sample stale; re-run Fit Models when you are satisfied with the evidence selection.
The comparison drawer
The drawer shows Transmission Domain and Appearance Domain side by side; there is no domain selector. Each domain aligns the extracted strip or strip diagram with Measured, Predicted (Color Model V2), Predicted (Color Model V1), and a per-swatch Prediction Error graph. The graph is Euclidean OKLab distance, with a fixed display scale and reference landmarks; it is a comparison aid, not a fit-quality acceptance gate.
The Color Corrections: On/Off toggle switches both models between their corrected and uncorrected predictions. That display preference is kept in browser session storage and does not mutate a fit. Measured appearance comes from the accepted extraction. Model predictions originate in linear transmission; their appearance rows require the current Camera Transform, so appearance predictions report unavailable if that transform cannot be loaded. See Transmission vs Appearance, Color Model v1, and Color Model v2.
Per-swatch exclusion
The drawer’s Swatch Exclusion module is a strip-shaped grid. Each variable-layer cell shows its nominal thickness and whether it is included; excluding a swatch requires confirmation, while including it is immediate. These are the same persistent fit controls exposed on the sample’s Logbook record. A partly excluded sample receives an N swatches excluded Fit State pill and appears under Has Excluded Swatches. A sample containing any permanently excluded filament is marked Filament Excluded and is ineligible regardless of its own sample/swatch controls.

Filaments — is each filament well covered?
The Filaments subtab answers a different question: does every filament have enough eligible evidence to be modeled? It is a sortable coverage table with columns Filament, Brand, Samples, Fit Samples, Incl. Swatches, Excl. Swatches, and Health. Health is a colored pill with this precedence:

Good — at least eight included swatches, provided none of the higher-priority states applies.
Sparse — fewer than eight included swatches.
Excluded only — the filament appears in accepted samples, but none of those samples is currently model-eligible.
Excluded — the filament carries the standing Exclude from model fits flag from Managing filaments.
Stale — one or more registered models is stale; this takes precedence over Sparse and Excluded only, but not the filament’s own Excluded state.

Clicking a row opens the filament detail drawer: Summary contains the persistent Exclude from Fits / Include in Fits action, Coverage reports included/total sample and swatch counts, Model State repeats the three registered-model states, and Samples lists every accepted sample containing the filament. Excluding a filament requires confirmation. Show In Samples jumps to the Samples subtab pre-filtered to this filament.
Read this tab as a gap-finder: a Sparse or Excluded only filament is a signal to print and calibrate more strips for it, or to re-include a sample you sidelined too aggressively.

The usual loop

Overview — clear Needs Attention (accept pending extractions upstream, resolve stale/missing).
Samples — spot-check suspect rows in the comparison drawer, Exclude the bad ones.
Filaments — check for Sparse / Excluded only coverage; re-include or plan more strips.
Fit Models — replace Color Model v1 and v2, and replace the Camera Transform when its preflight schedules it.
Publish Models — after all three are current, copy the exact current set into a new immutable library; activate it later through Generator’s Model Library → Manage control.

prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.title: Using the Calibration App
prisma-calibration/technical-reference/u.content:
The calibration app is a logbook. You register filaments and sample geometries, create samples, attach each sample its lightbox photographs, extract per-swatch color measurements, curate which measurements the models are allowed to trust, and fit the three working model families that a published Generator library requires. This section is the operator’s manual for that workflow — the screens, the controls, and the order of operations.
How It Works explains the phenomena behind each step; the Technical Reference is the code-level map. This tier stays at the level of what you click and why.
Running the app
In the packaged Suite, double-click Prisma Calibration.exe on Windows or run Prisma Calibration from the extracted Suite folder on Linux. The launcher creates or validates Calibration’s portable Workspace, starts the local server on port 8016 (or the next available local port), and asks the host to open the browser. Keep its console or terminal open while you work; closing it stops Calibration. See Launching the Calibration App for the complete user-facing procedure.
The app is a single-page frontend served by a FastAPI backend. It is a single-user, single-process tool: browser tabs share one live state and one database. Long operations have per-family job registries and explicit resource reservations; work that touches the same data is blocked, but there is no universal one-job-at-a-time lock. Source users should start Prisma.calibration_launcher so the portable SQLite and asset-root contract is established before server import. The window header reads Calibration Logbook.
The workspace at a glance
A topbar of global actions sits above five mode tabs:





























TabWhat you do thereLogbookThe master sample table. Create samples; open any sample to inspect or edit it.ImagesTwo subtabs: Assign Images (attach photos and blanks to samples) and Processing Queue (run extraction, then accept or reject the result).FilamentsThe filament library. Add and edit filaments and their print/model policy.GeometriesThe sample-geometry library. Define strip layouts, manage bundles, export files.ModelingCurate which samples and swatches feed the models, then fit them.
The topbar carries Refresh Data, Maintenance, and Backup / Restore.
The pages
Start here for the whole workflow end to end:

Driving the calibration app — the spine: how a sample goes from an idea to a fitted model, and how the app is wired underneath.

The library — the reusable things samples are built from:

Managing filaments — adding filaments and setting their white-cap, special-role, and model-exclusion policy.
Samples and geometries — defining strip geometries, managing bundles, and bulk-creating samples.

Measurement — turning photographs into color numbers:

Assigning images — the three-pane assign workspace, registering blanks, and bulk CSV assignment.
Processing and extraction — running extraction, handling failures with manual corner-picking, and accepting or rejecting results.

Modeling — deciding what the models learn:

The Modeling page — the Overview, Samples, and Filaments subtabs; excluding and including evidence; fitting the models.

Upkeep — keeping the library healthy:

Running maintenance — the maintenance dialog, and the staged re-extraction review.
Backup and restore — backup tiers, RAW-image archiving, and restoring.
