prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Preview CardModesAdvancedModesImprovinga Solve


The Advanced button at the end of the mode bar reveals two extra views. They’re diagnostic — most prints never need them — but they answer specific questions the everyday modes can’t.
Thickness Maps
One map per colored filament in the palette shows how thick that filament is laid down across the print. The grid also always includes three separate white-cap cards: Total, Boundary, and Detail. The Inferno scale runs from dark for lower values toward yellow-white for higher values; each card reports its maximum thickness and active-pixel count.
Use it to see what each filament is contributing — for example, whether an expensive color is barely used, or which filament is producing an unexpected region.
Click a card to open it in a lightbox. Its header stays fixed while the image changes size; use the Min–Max Zoom slider or the mouse wheel over the lightbox.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Thickness Maps grid showing the per-filament maps for a solved run.


Highpass
Shows only the parts of the print’s surface above a height you choose with the Threshold slider, and reports how many layers that leaves. Slide it down and the tallest features appear first.
Use it to spot isolated tall spikes — small lonely peaks print poorly, and this view finds them before the printer does.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Highpass view with the threshold pulled partway down so only the tallest features show.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How To Use/Preview/Improving a Solve.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.title: Improving a Solve
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}AdvancedModesImprovinga SolveExport


A disappointing preview does not necessarily mean that the solver failed. The selected palette may be a poor fit for the image, or one small part of an otherwise good solve may need a controlled nudge. The most reliable procedure is to explore broadly with palettes first, then make narrow settings changes only after choosing a promising palette.
There is no single numerical score that captures everything people notice in an image. Use Suggest dE and RMSE % as screening information, but choose by comparing the predicted images at full size.
The short version

Add several strong suggestions to the Palette Deck, switch the top-bar action to Batch Solve, and select them.
Keep the palette with the best overall cohesion, even if another run has a slightly better score.
Identify one specific defect in that run.
Make one small settings change aimed at that defect.
Solve again and compare both runs side by side.
Keep the change only when the preview is meaningfully better.

If the whole image feels wrong, return to the palette before changing many settings. If the image is already close and only one feature is wrong, keep the palette and use the targeted adjustments below.
The ordinary starting posture
Prisma’s defaults incorporate the broadly useful settings from the production-scale comparison:

Appearance budget: 0.004 dE
Smoothing radius: 1.0 mm
Min Cap Layers: 2
Boundary mutation: enabled, with one pass
White-point rescale: disabled

These defaults are intended to produce a strong first solve, not to be universally optimal. In particular, white-point rescaling remains opt-in because it can produce a major improvement when an image needs greater internal color coherence, but it changes the image’s absolute color target and is not a universal win.
Optional refinement profiles
Prisma includes two evidence-backed alternatives under Settings → Profiles…:

Refinement — Balanced is the safer first comparison. It enables Print-Scale Smoothing, uses a 0.4 mm solve pitch, 2.0 mm cap smoothing, a 3.5 mm thickness limit, nine detail layers, and two boundary-mutation passes.
Refinement — Strong changes the solve more aggressively. It uses the same preprocessing and cap policy, with a 3.0 mm thickness limit, four colors per region, coarser first-stage planning, five detail layers, and three mutation passes.

These are conditional alternatives, not higher quality levels and not automatic fallbacks. Compare Balanced first when the ordinary result is promising but unresolved; try Strong when you want a more substantial alternate interpretation. Loading either profile intentionally changes the solve pitch and several other settings while retaining the standard 1.0 mm smoothing radius.
First, compare palettes
Palette choice usually changes the result more than a reasonable adjustment to one solver setting. Prisma’s first suggestion is a strong starting point, but the suggestion order estimates color coverage before the full solve. It cannot completely predict region boundaries, white-cap seams, or whether a coherent color cast will look better than one locally accurate but distracting color.
Use this palette pass:

In Palette → Auto-Suggest, set Suggestions to the number you want to inspect (usually the default 5) and press Suggest Palettes.
Add the promising suggestions to the Palette Deck. You may also include a manual, saved, or previously loaded palette.
Use the arrow beside the top-bar Solve action to choose Batch Solve, then check 2–10 deck cards.
Leave the image and settings unchanged, press Batch Solve (N), and confirm the full-solve batch.
In Preview, compare results as they complete and click each predicted image when you need the full-resolution view.

Judge the image in this order:

Does the image read correctly as a whole?
Are broad skies, walls, skin, fabric, or other familiar surfaces internally coherent?
Is any small region so wrong that it attracts attention?
Are there conspicuous seams, false outlines, or speckled patches?
Only then, which remaining run follows the source most closely?

A lower Suggest dE or RMSE % is useful evidence, not a command. A slightly less literal palette can look better when its errors are consistent across the image.
The deck cards remain available after the comparison. Switch back to
Single Solve and click the palette you want to refine. If you want to keep
the solved result itself across a Prisma restart, press Save on its Preview
card.
To test a nearby palette rather than rebuilding it, open the promising Palette
Deck card’s ⋯ menu and choose Create Variant. Manual mode receives an
ordered copy; replace the filament you want to test and press Add Variant to
Deck. The source remains intact, so both cards can immediately be selected
for another Batch Solve.
Then, name the defect
Avoid changing settings merely because a run is not perfect. Describe the visible problem first and choose the smallest matching intervention.













































What you seeWhat to try firstWhat the change is doingSmooth sky, wall, skin, or fabric looks chunky or steppedConfirm Appearance budget is 0.004 dE, especially after loading an older Settings Profile; if it is, compare another paletteThe lower default protects appearance more aggressively while the boundary cap is smoothed, but palette choice remains the stronger interventionRegion edges or white-cap seams look too starkRaise Min Cap Layers from 2 to 3Adds another small optical buffer above the colors, which can soften the apparent transitionDark or strongly colored regions look too boldTry Min Cap Layers from 3 to 5Uses more of the available height for white, selectively weakening regions that were consuming much of the color-height budgetBroad regions have an inconsistent cast, or one part of a familiar object has an alien hueCompare a run with White-point rescale: EnabledRemaps the image around the printable white point and can make the solved image more internally coherentBoundary-cap smoothing creates dark outlines around raised areasReduce Smoothing radius from 1.0 toward 0.5 mmLimits how far height differences are blended into neighboring regionsAn almost-excellent solve has one small, glaring boundary defectTry Noise Reduction: Light, one additional advanced Mutation pass, or one additional Min Cap LayerProduces a nearby solution that may escape one locally plausible but visually awkward choiceFine detail is missing and the print is constrained by its maximum thicknessTry a Detail depth of 9 layersGives the detail cap more vertical room; it usually adds little when thickness is not the limiting factor
These are starting points, not a recipe to apply all at once.
Why some useful changes score worse
Human vision is unusually tolerant of a coherent change in lighting or overall color cast. The same object can look normal at noon or near sunset even though its measured colors are very different. An erratic color change within one familiar object is much more distracting.
That is why White-point rescale can make a preview look better while its literal source-error score gets worse. It may sacrifice absolute color matching to bring outlier regions into agreement with the rest of the solved image. Keep it off when the ordinary solve is already coherent; compare it when pale, neutral, or familiar regions disagree with one another.
The same principle applies when choosing palettes. Prefer the result that forms one believable image over a result that matches one isolated color perfectly but makes that region look detached from its surroundings.
Use cap layers deliberately
Min Cap Layers is more than a coverage safeguard:

2 layers is the ordinary default; it gently softens region boundaries and reduces the perceptual prominence of lateral white-cap coverage.
3–5 layers can calm dark or saturated areas that look too forceful.
1 layer preserves the greatest available color height when maximum contrast or saturation matters more.

Additional minimum cap layers do much less to already-light regions because those regions were not using much color height in the first place. Watch the predicted image rather than assuming the whole result will become uniformly washed out.
Nudge a nearly excellent solve
When only one small feature is wrong—especially a face or another familiar shape—the solver may have made a locally reasonable choice that people notice as a defect. Large global changes are risky at this point.
Instead, create a few nearby alternatives:

use Noise Reduction: Light to make a very small change to the source entering the solve;
add one Mutation pass so an existing region boundary gets another chance to move;
or add one Min Cap Layer to slightly soften the color-height result.

Try these separately before combining them. Their purpose is not to improve every metric; it is to give a nearly successful solve another path around one objectionable local result.
Changes that deserve caution

Do not change many unrelated controls in one run. You will not know which change helped, and interactions can hide a new defect.
Do not keep increasing smoothing. A larger radius can help a calm area while creating a dark lateral-cap outline around a neighboring raised region.
Do not enable White-point rescale by default for every image. It is powerful precisely because it changes the rendering target.
Do not chase a tiny score improvement when the image looks less coherent.
Do not use strong preprocessing merely to remove normal photographic texture. Overprocessing can replace natural variation with broad artificial patches.

A repeatable comparison loop
Name runs for the question they test—for example, Sky – palette 3, Cap budget 0.004, or White-point rescale. Keep the current best run visible beside each new candidate. Inspect both the whole composition and the problem area at full size.
Stop when the remaining differences are merely different compromises. The predicted appearance does not need to reproduce noisy source pixels exactly; the goal is a coherent image without a conspicuous local failure.

This guidance comes from production-scale comparisons across varied real images, palettes of three to five colors, and expert visual review. The controlled study used no-swap palettes and a 0.4 mm nozzle with 0.4 mm solve pitch. Treat the procedures as strong starting points rather than guarantees for every image, palette, or print setup.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreviewPreview CardModesAdvancedModes


The bar above the preview switches what a solved run displays. Predicted is the everyday view; the others show the physical print behind it. Where a view maps thickness or height, a scale bar below explains the colors, and views with sub-options show them in a row under the mode bar. Click any image to enlarge it. Ordinary image lightboxes have a fixed header and a Min–Max Zoom slider; the image scales beneath the controls, which stay in place while you drag.
Predicted
What the print should look like lit from behind — the app’s best prediction of the finished lithophane. This is the view to judge results by: compare it against the source column and decide with your eye.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Predicted view beside the source image.


White Cap
Maps of the white cap’s thickness — brighter means thicker white. View picks which part:

Total — the whole cap.
Boundary — just the continuous covering layer.
Detail — just the fine relief on top.

All three use the same Inferno thickness scale: dark purple marks lower values and yellow-white marks higher values. The consistent palette makes Total, Boundary, and Detail directly interpretable without assigning a special color meaning to one component.
Contours: On/Off overlays lines marking each printed-layer step. In Luminance mode this view shows where the image’s brightness structure is being carried by white thickness.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The White Cap view with the Total/Boundary/Detail selector and contours on.


Color Regions
Two looks at the color stack under the cap, switched by View:

Color Ceiling — a height map of where the colored layers top out across the print.
Recipe Viewer — the print rendered from its colors alone, plus the “cookbook”: which filament combination produces each region. Click around to see what’s actually printed where — useful when a color surprises you and you want to know which filaments made it.



                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Recipe Viewer with a region’s recipe visible.


Top Surface
The final printable outer surface — the actual heights the printer will build, everything included. Contours: On/Off marks the layer steps. This is the closest thing to holding the unlit print and looking across it.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Top Surface view with contours on.


Explorer
A horizontal slice through the print: pick a Height with the slider and see which material sits at that height everywhere in the print, within a Band ± window you can widen or narrow. Like peeling the print down to a chosen layer — the way to answer “what is the printer putting down at 1.4 mm?”


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Explorer view mid-height, with the Height and Band controls visible.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.title: Preview
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SettingsPreviewExportPreview CardModesAdvancedModesImprovinga Solve


The Preview tab is where lithophanes actually get built and judged. You start a solve, Prisma works out the filament stack for every point, and the results land here for inspection — before you’ve spent any plastic.
A lot happens under the hood during a solve; you don’t need any of it to use the app. If you’re curious, How It Works explains the whole machine.
Starting a solve
Press the main part of Solve in the top bar. In Single Solve mode it
needs a selected image and an active Palette Deck card. The adjacent arrow
switches to Batch Solve, where you check 2–10 deck cards and press the main
button to confirm a sequence of full solves. Choosing a mode never starts work.
Progress shows while the solve runs; you can cancel and keep using the app.
If Solve Pitch is smaller than the active nozzle diameter, Prisma explains the mismatch and offers to set the pitch to that exact diameter before continuing. Cancel leaves the setting unchanged. Other blocking settings problems still need to be resolved manually because they may have more than one valid correction.
A batch uses one frozen image, settings, preprocessing, printer/nozzle, model
library, and white base/cap snapshot, then changes only the colored palette.
It can compare deck cards of different origins and sizes. Prisma deliberately
does not choose a winner.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Preview tab with a completed solve: the source and predicted result side by side, the view-mode bar above, and the Solve History column on the right.


Preview cards
A finished solve appears as columns in the main area — your source photo beside the solved result. The bar above switches what the result shows: the predicted appearance, the white cap, the color regions, and more. Each view is described in Preview Card Modes; the extra diagnostic views behind the Advanced button are in Advanced Modes. Source Image: On/Off hides the source column when you want more room. Click any image to enlarge it.
In ordinary image and thickness-map lightboxes, the header stays fixed at the top while only the image changes size. Drag the Zoom slider from Min to Max, or scroll the mouse wheel over the lightbox. Min shows the image at its native pixel size when that fits (otherwise it fits the viewport); Max fills the available viewer area without putting the header or image outside the screen. Explorer, Highpass, and Recipe Viewer keep their own view-specific controls instead of using this image-zoom control.
One thing to know up front: the result can look blocky compared with the photo. That view shows the solve grid honestly rather than inventing image detail between solved points. A field-derived white-cap export may reconstruct a smoother physical cap surface, but it does not create new color decisions beyond the solve resolution.
Solve History
Every solve becomes a card in the Solve History column on the right, newest
on top. Each card shows the run’s name, its palette colors, and RMSE %, the
run’s overall color-error score. Lower is closer to the target, but use the
predicted image rather than the number alone when choosing between runs.
Settings opens the read-only settings captured for that solve.
Click a card to show or hide that run in the main area. You can also focus a
card and press Enter or Space. Showing two or more runs puts them side by side
— the easiest way to judge whether a settings or palette change actually
helped. Export uses the same card family but selects one completed run at a
time.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

Two Solve History cards selected, with both runs displayed side by side next to the source.


Batch cards can show Queued, Solving, or Failed until they finish.
A failed card keeps its concise error and can be deleted; later batch items
continue. To keep a completed run deliberately, save it. Save is available after the solve
finishes. Clear removes the cards from the current Solve History display
only. It asks for a second click and is unavailable while the history is empty
or a solve/export prevents clearing. It does not delete automatic saves,
explicitly saved runs, or the completed run artifacts retained by Generator’s
separate cache policy during the current Prisma process.
Saving and loading solves
Press Save on a card and give it a name to keep that run permanently —
result, settings, palette, everything. Names such as Run 7 are reserved for
the automatic labels Generator gives new live cards, so choose a descriptive
name instead.
Load (top of Solve History) opens the Saved Runs window: your saved runs plus recent automatic saves from this Prisma process (ordinary successful solves are auto-saved on a best-effort basis). Select one to Load it back — it behaves exactly like a run you just solved, including being exportable. Save keeps an automatic save permanently, Rename and Delete manage the list, Download hands you the run as a file, and Load from file… brings a downloaded run back in — handy as a backup or to move a run to another computer.
Unsaved run artifacts and automatic saves are session-temporary and are
removed when a newly launched Prisma process starts. Use Save, download, or
export for anything that must survive a restart.
Prisma keeps the archived source privately with the loaded card. When an
Image Library photo has exactly the same bytes, Prisma reuses that photo as
the active image; otherwise the Image tab shows a temporary Saved run
source without adding another file to the Library. Re-saving the loaded card
still embeds the archive’s original image bytes even if a reused Library file
is later changed or deleted.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Saved Runs window with a few saved and automatic runs listed.




                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Rename saved run dialog.


When the result isn’t right
Compare the predicted view against the source and trust your eye. Start with several strong palette suggestions before tuning settings: palette choice usually changes more than one reasonable solver adjustment. Once you have a promising palette, name the specific defect, change one matching control, solve again, and compare both runs side by side.
Improving a Solve provides the full procedure and targeted starting points for chunky gradients, white-cap seams, overly bold dark regions, incoherent color casts, smoothing outlines, and isolated local defects.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/r.title: Runs with Swaps
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/r.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteRuns withSwapsSettings


A run needs swaps when its palette contains more colored filaments than the active printer has color slots. Prisma plans these runs automatically; there is no separate mode or setting to choose.
Swaps increase the available palette, but they are not a free upgrade. The solve takes longer, the band structure consumes part of the thickness budget, white fill between bands can dilute color, and the print requires correctly timed filament changes. A palette that fits in one load is the more reliable baseline and will generally produce an equal or better result when it can cover the image well enough.
Before solving

Open Configuration and confirm the active printer, material-system units, and slot count.
Select the white filament under Settings → Essentials. White occupies a slot throughout the print.
Build a palette that exceeds the remaining color slots. In Auto-Suggest, set Palette colors above the displayed simultaneous capacity. In Manual mode, simply select the additional colors.
Keep a no-swap palette available when possible so you can compare whether the extra colors actually help.



                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

Auto-Suggest with Palette colors above the active printer’s simultaneous capacity, showing the capacity warning and an oversized suggested palette.


Solve and compare
Press Solve normally. Prisma first runs a lower-resolution scout to estimate how the image uses the palette, then plans the swap bands and runs the final solve. This takes longer than a run whose palette fits at once.
On Preview, compare the swap run with the no-swap baseline. Look at the predicted image, not only RMSE %. Extra colors are useful when they make a visible improvement in important parts of the image; a slightly better score alone may not justify the added constraints and print handling.
The swap plan is fixed as part of the completed run. If you change the printer’s slot capacity, solve again under the new configuration.
Generate Swap Instructions

Open 4 Export and select the completed swap run.
Under Swap Instructions, press Generate.
Confirm the initial slot assignments and each later unload/load instruction.
Use Copy to Clipboard to carry the plan into OrcaSlicer.
Generate the print files from the same selected run.

Swap-instruction generation is a short request that runs to completion once started. Its progress bar does not offer a misleading Cancel action.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

Swap Instructions for a completed run, including the initial slot loading, pause heights, and per-slot changes.


Follow the slot identities and pause heights exactly. The instructions assume the printer configuration used for the solve and do not redesign the plan at export time.
Practical guidance

Prefer the smallest palette that gives a meaningful visual improvement.
Increase Palette colors deliberately; larger searches take longer, and an oversized palette may add print handling without improving the result.
Keep the white filament loaded in its assigned slot for the entire print.
Check that each required filament is ready before slicing and printing.
Treat a swap run as a deliberate second option, not the default path for every image.

For the reason the solve uses flat filament bands and white fill, see Runs with Swaps in How It Works.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How To Use/Settings/Color Solver.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: Color Solver Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreprocessingModulesColorSolverWhiteCap


These control the heart of the process: how Prisma decides which filaments to stack, and how thick, at every point of the print. The section has two parts — how colors are matched (Recipe Search) and how the image is carved into color patches (Region Construction).


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Color Solver section of the settings drawer with Advanced: On, showing both the Recipe Search and Region Construction tables.


Appearance Model
The calibrated prediction of what color a stack of filaments makes when backlit. Color Model v2 (default) is the newer, more accurate model; Color Model v1 is the older one, kept for comparison. This choice affects everything downstream — the solve, the suggested palettes, and every preview.
Recipe Search

Out-of-gamut handling (advanced) — what happens to photo colors your palette simply can’t make. Nearest reachable color (default) substitutes the closest color the palette can print. Preserve hue keeps the hue, mutes the vividness, and nudges brightness only when a color is too dark or bright to print — often gentler on skin tones and skies.
White-point rescale (off by default) — scales the image so its white matches the brightest white the print can make. It can improve internal color coherence when pale tints or parts of a familiar object disagree, even when literal source-error metrics get worse. It is opt-in because it changes the absolute color target and is not a universal improvement.
Color corrections — applies the calibration’s measured correction data when predicting stack colors. Leave on; turning it off makes predictions less accurate.
Max colors per region — how many different colored filaments may stack at a single point (1–7). More lets tricky colors be mixed better, but slows the solve and makes busier stacks. 3 is a good middle.
Color mismatch tolerance (advanced) — how far off a color must be before it counts as unreachable and gets remapped. The difference is measured as dE (delta E), a perceptual color-difference estimate; lower is stricter.
Chroma weight (advanced) — a slider from Tone to Color. Center is balanced; drag toward Color to make the matching favor hue and vividness, toward Tone to favor brightness. Each step doubles or halves the weight shown.

Region Construction
Prisma doesn’t pick a recipe per pixel — it first divides the image into small color patches (regions) and solves those. These settings set how that patchwork is drawn.

Region method (advanced) — how regions are drawn. Image regions (default) and Superpixels follow the picture’s own structure; Fixed grid uses uniform squares.
Region planning scale (advanced) — plan the regions on a coarser version of the image (1× = full resolution). Higher makes broader, simpler regions and faster solves, but follows fine edges less closely.
Color region target — the intended size of a color patch, in millimeters. Smaller follows the image more faithfully; larger gives simpler, cleaner prints.
Neutral-field protection (advanced, off by default) — reduces abrupt hue shifts between nearly identical weakly colored regions, especially in cloudy skies and shaded neutral backgrounds. Narrow, Standard, and Broad progressively include more source colors; they change the protection’s scope, not its strength. Start with Standard. Broad may also influence pale skin and subtly colored subjects, so compare its preview with Off before printing.
Local recipe corrections (advanced) — lets small spots inside a region use a better-matching recipe when the improvement is strong. Preserves fine detail, at the cost of more small patches. On by default.

Boundary mutation
Boundary mutation (advanced) lets boundary points borrow a recipe from the region immediately across the border when that recipe matches the photo better. It is on by default. The change is accepted in connected boundary runs, so the result shifts a contour instead of scattering unrelated points.

Mutation passes — the maximum number of refinement passes (1–16). Each pass can move the boundary one solve point farther; processing stops early when nothing else improves.
Mutation current-dE percentile — only consider boundary points whose current dE is among the worst. Empty considers all boundary candidates; the cutoff is recalculated each pass.
Mutation min gain — the minimum average color-error improvement a connected run must achieve. Empty uses the default shown in the field.
Mutation min contact — the minimum length along which a proposed run must touch the region whose recipe it borrows. Raising it rejects short, weakly attached shifts.

Figures for review

Image regions form unequal patches around image structure; Superpixels favor compact patches that still follow edges; Fixed grid uses uniform cells regardless of the picture.

Boundary mutation refines an existing recipe boundary; it does not introduce a new recipe. Each pass can advance a boundary by one solve point.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How To Use/Settings/Preprocessing Module Settings.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: Preprocessing Module Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SettingsPreprocessingModulesColorSolver


Preprocessing changes the image before color solving starts. It can reduce noise, simplify detail that will not survive printing, or move tones and saturation toward what the selected palette can reproduce. These are creative controls as much as cleanup tools: use the preview and compare runs rather than assuming stronger is better.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Pre-processing section of the settings drawer, with the module toggles visible and one module set to Custom so its fields show.


Resample kernel (advanced)
How the photo is shrunk onto the solve grid. Lanczos (default) keeps things sharper; Area gives a softer, smoother result that can suit coarse prints. It only matters when the photo is larger than the solve grid — which it almost always is.
The modules
Five modules run in a fixed order, each switched on or off independently:
Noise Reduction → Print-Scale Smoothing → Flat-Area Smoothing → Palette Tone Fit → Palette Saturation Fit
All five start off on a fresh install. Each module has strength presets plus Off and Custom; picking Custom reveals its individual fields. The first three change spatial detail. The last two change the target’s tone or saturation and do nothing until a palette exists.
Noise Reduction
Softens fine grain and noise while trying to preserve edges. It is a useful first step when texture or sensor noise is fragmenting the solved color regions. Custom fields:

Filter radius — how large an area each point is smoothed over.
Color similarity — how different two colors can be and still get blended. Higher smooths across stronger color differences.
Spatial reach — how far the smoothing extends, in pixels.

Print-Scale Smoothing
Off by default. Smooths away detail finer than your printer can physically render, producing larger, simpler color patches. Its strength automatically tracks your nozzle size and solve pitch. Custom fields:

Feature scale — scales the smoothing radius: below 1 keeps more detail, above 1 flattens more.
Color similarity — as above.
Passes — how many times the smoothing is applied.

Flat-Area Smoothing
Off by default. Collapses gradual texture into broad flat areas — at higher strengths the image takes on a painted, graphic look. Custom fields:

Flattening strength — how aggressively texture is flattened.
Scale strength to print width — ties the strength to your printer’s real resolution so it tracks what’s printable.
Flattening mode — what gets flattened: lightness only, lightness and color, or everything.
Iteration limit — a cap on how long the flattening computation runs.

Palette Tone Fit
Off by default. Needs a palette. Remaps the photo’s brightness range to the darkest and lightest your palette can physically print, so shadows and highlights land where the filaments can reach instead of being clipped. Custom fields:

Tone fit strength — how fully the remap is applied (0 = none, 1 = full).
Shadow anchor — how much of the darkest part of the image is treated as “black.”
Highlight anchor — how much of the brightest part is treated as “white.”
Midtone curve — bends the in-between tones lighter or darker.

Palette Saturation Fit
Off by default. Needs a palette. Gently pulls colors that are more vivid than your palette can print back within its reach, keeping their hue and brightness. Softer than letting the solver clip them. Custom fields:

Compression start — how close to the palette’s limit a color must be before it starts getting pulled in. Lower starts earlier and affects more of the image.
Compression softness — how gradual the pull-in is.

Figure for review

The first three modules simplify spatial detail in different ways. The palette-aware modules instead move tone or saturation toward what the selected palette can reproduce.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How To Use/Settings/White Cap.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: White Cap Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ColorSolverWhiteCapPreview


Every lithophane has a white cap above the color stack. The cap diffuses the backlight, affects the predicted appearance, and forms the viewing surface. It has two required parts: the boundary cap, which continuously covers the solved color stacks, and the detail cap, which adds localized white relief above that boundary where the image calls for it.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The White Cap section of the settings drawer with Advanced: On, showing the Boundary and Detail sub-sections.


Min Cap Layers
The minimum number of boundary-cap layers everywhere above the colors. Its minimum thickness is this count multiplied by Layer Height. The default is two layers, which provides a small optical buffer that can soften region boundaries and lateral-cap seams. The app permits no fewer than one layer so every solved color stack has continuous white cover.
Boundary

Shading balance (Luminance mode only) — where light-and-dark variation is carried. Toward Smooth, more of it goes into the broader boundary-cap surface; toward Detail, more goes into localized detail relief. Suggest proposes a balance from the selected image.
Boundary cap (advanced) — the cap’s character. Detail Aware (default) keeps the cap as thin as it can wherever thickening it would visibly change the image. Smooth prioritizes a clean, continuous outer surface instead.
Appearance budget (advanced, Detail Aware only) — how much visible color change you’ll tolerate in exchange for a smoother cap. The default is 0.004 dE; lower protects the image more aggressively.
Smoothing radius — how far the cap’s top surface is smoothed, in millimeters. The default is 1.0 mm. Lower keeps more tonal relief; higher gives a cleaner surface. It remains meaningful in both boundary-cap modes, and the cap’s underside always fits the colors exactly.

Detail

Detail depth — the maximum number of white layers the detail cap may add above the boundary cap. It is a limit, not a target: the detail cap can appear as separated bumps and ridges rather than covering the entire surface. At 0, the detail-cap stage still runs but has no extra height available to place.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteSettingsPreviewPreprocessingModulesColorSolverWhiteCap


Settings control how Prisma builds the lithophane — its thickness and resolution, any preprocessing applied to the image, how colors are matched, and how the white cap is built. The defaults are sensible: you can make a good print without opening this drawer at all.
The settings drawer
Press the Settings gear (top right) to slide the drawer in from the right — it works from any tab. Pills along the top of the drawer switch between sections: Essentials, Pre-processing, Color Solver, and White Cap. The square button expands the drawer to full width; the × closes it.
Advanced: Off / On (in the drawer header) hides or reveals the less-common settings. Leave it off at first — everything you need day to day is visible without it.


                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The settings drawer open on Essentials, with Advanced: Off — the section pills, the profile bar, the stack diagram, and the Essentials table.


There’s no OK or Apply — changes take hold as you make them, and they apply to the next solve. A solve already running or finished keeps the settings it started with. Exporting an older run uses that run’s frozen settings rather than whatever is currently in the drawer.
When improving an existing preview, follow Improving a Solve: compare several palettes before tuning, identify one visible defect, and change only the control aimed at that defect.
Profiles
The bar at the top of the drawer manages settings profiles — named saves of the entire settings collection. The current profile’s name is shown, with a marker when you’ve changed something since it was saved.

Profiles… opens the profiles window: pick a profile from the list to load it, or Restore System Defaults to go back to a factory state.
Save stores your current settings into the current profile.
Save As… stores them under a new name.



                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Settings Profiles window with a few profiles in the list.




                  
                  📸 Screenshot to capture 
                  
                

The Save Settings Profile As window.


Profiles are how you keep useful setups around — for example, a high-detail profile and a quicker draft profile — and switch between them in two clicks. When you find settings that work, save them.
Prisma ships two optional profiles derived from production-scale solve comparisons: Refinement — Balanced and Refinement — Strong. They are alternate solve recipes, not replacements for Basic and not guaranteed improvements. See Improving a Solve for their intended order and tradeoffs.
Essentials
The everyday section: the print’s physical envelope and the one big quality choice. The diagram at the top shows the stack these settings describe — white base on the bottom, color layers, white cap on top, viewed from the cap side.

Solve Mode — the biggest single choice in the app. Color aims the filament stacks directly at the image’s colors. Luminance lets white-cap thickness carry more of the image’s brightness and fine detail, with color underneath. Compare both when subtle light-and-dark structure matters; the better choice depends on the image and palette.
Solve Pitch — the size of one solve point, in millimeters. Smaller = more detail but slower solves and exports. It cannot be smaller than the active nozzle diameter. If a solve is blocked for that reason, Prisma offers to set it to the exact nozzle diameter and continue. Larger values remain valid when you intentionally want a coarser, faster solve.
Max Total Thickness — the print’s total thickness budget. Thicker gives the solver more layers to work with — deeper darks and richer color — at the cost of print time.
Layer Height — must exactly match the layer height you’ll slice with. If these disagree, the printed colors won’t match the preview.
White Base/Cap Filament — the white used for the solid base and the top cap. This is chosen here, not in the palette (see Palette).
Base Thickness — the solid white plate the print sits on.

The line under the table shows what these work out to — how many color layers the budget leaves, and the resulting stack.
The other sections
Each has its own page describing every setting and what it does to the print. The short version:

Preprocessing Module Settings — optional clean-up of the photo before solving: noise reduction, smoothing toward printable detail, and reshaping tones and saturation toward what your palette can reproduce. Each module is a simple preset picker; all start off.
Color Solver — how colors are matched. The everyday controls: the Appearance Model (the calibrated color prediction — v2 is the default), Color corrections (leave on), Max colors per region (how many filaments may stack in one spot), and Color region target (how fine the color patchwork is).
White Cap — the white layer above the colors. Day to day: Min Cap Layers (default 2; minimum 1) and, in Luminance mode, Shading balance (whether broad shading comes from smooth cap thickness or fine relief).

There is no separate swap-planning setting. When a palette needs more colors than your printer can hold at once, Prisma plans the required filament bands automatically during the solve. See Runs with Swaps for when to use them and how to carry the plan into the slicer.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.title: How To Use
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.content:
.htu-diagram svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-diagram a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-diagram a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-diagram a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Set up onceMake each lithophaneConfigurationImagePaletteSettingsPreviewExport3D Printing


A color lithophane is a thin printed panel that reveals a color image when lit from behind. You give Prisma a photo and the filaments available to you; it works out a printable stack and exports the files your slicer needs.
This section is the practical guide to the app. It explains what to do and what each choice changes. For a conceptual view of the machinery underneath, see How It Works.
The workflow in the app
The conceptual workflow and the controls are nearly the same, but a few decisions live outside the numbered tabs:





































In the appWhat you are decidingConfiguration in the left railWhich calibrated filaments and printer setup are available. This is mostly one-time setup.1 ImageWhich image area to print, its physical size, and any image adjustments.2 PaletteWhich colored filaments the solve may use.Settings gearOptional solve, preprocessing, region, and white-cap behavior for the next run.Solve → 3 PreviewBuild a run, inspect the prediction, and compare it with earlier runs.4 ExportChoose a completed run and generate its 3MF or STL files and any Swap Instructions.3D PrintingMove the generated files into the slicer, prepare the printer, and light the finished panel.
Most iteration happens between Palette, Settings, and Preview. Change one meaningful thing, solve again, and compare the runs side by side.

New here? Getting Started covers installing and launching the app and walks through a first solve.

Appearance
Use the Theme control in the right side of the top bar, beside Clear Temp Files, to choose System, Light, or Dark. System follows your operating-system appearance, including changes made while Generator is open; an explicit Light or Dark choice stays fixed. Generator saves the preference in this browser and synchronizes it between open Generator tabs. It is an interface preference only—not part of Settings Profiles, saved runs, or exports.
Setup

Configuration — tell Prisma which filaments you own and which printer setup is active.

Make a lithophane

Image — choose a photo, set the physical print size, and frame it.
Palette — choose colored filaments manually or ask Prisma to suggest them.
Settings — tune print thickness, solve behavior, preprocessing, and the white cap when needed.
Preview — build and compare predicted results.
Improving a Solve — compare palettes first, then use targeted settings changes for specific visible defects.
Export — generate print files for a selected completed run.

Special workflow

Runs with Swaps — use more colored filaments than the printer can hold at once and carry the resulting Swap Instructions into the slicer.

After export

3D Printing — slice, print, and light the result.
Tutorials — worked examples from start to finish.

Clear Temp Files in the top bar removes accumulated working files, solve
and export history, automatic saves, temporary saved-run sources, and internal
caches—including prepared copies of HEIC, HEIF, and AVIF sources. It never
deletes originals in Generator/Images, exported files, or runs you explicitly
saved. If a temporary saved-run source was active, load that saved run again
to restore it. Prepared conversion copies are rebuilt when an image is next
needed or the library is refreshed.
A newly launched Prisma process also clears session-temporary cache—unsaved
solves, batch artifacts, Auto Runs, LUTs, and temporary imports—but preserves
prepared source conversions so HEIC/HEIF/AVIF images do not needlessly
reconvert. Explicitly saved runs and exports survive. Reconnecting to an
already-running process does not trigger this cleanup.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Color-core library
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: Prisma/lib/ contains several low-level color, transmission, stack-geometry, registry, and Camera Transform helpers, but their liveness differs substantially—some are central to the current product, some are used only by Calibration, and some are compatibility or reference utilities with no production caller.

This page distinguishes the reusable code from the code that the current Generator and Calibration paths actually call. The modules are mostly framework-free, but they do not form one uniformly live “core.”
Liveness map



































ModuleCurrent statusMain consumerslib.transmissionLiveGenerator model/LUT/palette/preprocessing paths, photo-stack prediction, and some Calibration physical-stack codelib.stack_geometryPartly liveGenerator appearance prediction, photo-stack prediction, and Calibration fittinglib.camera_transformLiveGenerator ingress/display conversion and Calibration Camera Transform fitting/bakinglib.colorMostly dormantlinear_to_hex is live in Calibration modeling review; the other helpers have no current production importerlib.filamentsTest/reference-onlyCurrent whole-repo callers are tests; the apps use their own model-library/catalog loaders
Related architecture nodes: lib.transmission, lib.color, lib.stack_geometry, lib.filaments, and lib.camera_transform.
Two ΔE definitions—and two liveness caveats
The repository contains two non-interchangeable helper functions:




















FunctionSpace and formulaLiveness of this exact helperlib.transmission.deltaE_ok(lab1, lab2)Euclidean distance in OKLabDormant: the product performs equivalent vectorized OKLab distances directly, but has no current caller of this helperlib.color.compute_dE_from_linear(measured, predicted)Convert linear RGB to CIE Lab, then compute CIE76Dormant copy: Calibration calls the duplicate in calibration/fitting/color_math.py
The underlying metrics are live even though these two exact wrappers are not. Generator solving and palette suggestion compare colors in OKLab. Calibration fitting uses its own CIE-Lab/CIE76 implementation. A numeric value from one space must not be treated as interchangeable with the same number from the other.
Stable source anchors: linear_to_oklab, oklab_to_linear, and deltaE_ok in lib/transmission.py; linear_to_lab and compute_dE_from_linear in lib/color.py; the active Calibration duplicate in calibration/fitting/color_math.py.
OKLab conversion (lib/transmission.py)





















FunctionContractlinear_to_oklab(rgb_linear)Vectorized linear-sRGB (..., 3) to OKLab using the hard-coded Ottosson matricesoklab_to_linear(lab)Vectorized OKLab to linear sRGB; clips the result to [0, 1]deltaE_ok(lab1, lab2)Scalar Euclidean OKLab distance; currently has no production caller
Because oklab_to_linear clips at the RGB cube, an out-of-gamut OKLab value does not round-trip losslessly. Generator model.to_oklab wraps linear_to_oklab and returns float32.
Scalar color helpers (lib/color.py)
This module uses scalar/std-lib math rather than the vectorized NumPy path.








































FunctionContractCurrent uselinear_to_srgbExact piecewise sRGB encoding to an 8-bit channelIndirectly live through linear_to_hexlinear_to_hexLinear RGB to #RRGGBBLive in Calibration modeling reviewsrgb_to_linearInverse piecewise sRGB transferNo current production importerlinear_to_labApproximate D65 linear-RGB to CIE LabNo current production importer of this copycompute_dE_from_linearCIE76 after linear_to_labNo current production importer of this copyinterp_single, interpolate_pchipScalar interpolation/extrapolation utilitiesNo current production importer of these copies
Calibration fitting carries and calls corresponding implementations in calibration/fitting/color_math.py; it does not import these functions from lib.color.
Spline transmission model (lib/transmission.py)
This is the canonical Generator-side historical spline model. Measured (thickness, T_rgb) knots are interpolated channel-by-channel with monotone PCHIP. Composition multiplies layer transmissions; optional pair corrections can then modify the result.
Build and predict

























FunctionContractbuild_splineBuilds one PCHIP per RGB channel, requires the first knot at 0.0, disables PCHIP extrapolation, and clips transmission to [0, 1]predictReturns unity at non-positive thickness, spline interpolation in-range, and _extrapolate beyond the final knot_get_splinesLazily builds and caches splines in profile['_splines']_extrapolateExtends the last measured segment with a Beer–Lambert-style log slope
Despite their leading underscores, _get_splines and _extrapolate are part of the practical Generator contract. Current callers include palette/suggest.py, the legacy fixed-color helper in lut.py, and live staged-solver helpers. Calibration has separate fitting-side implementations.
Compose and corrections
compose(layers, corrections=None) multiplies predict(profile, thickness) over an ordered layer sequence and clips the final RGB. When corrections are enabled, it derives the lookup key from the first layer as the overlay and the remaining layers as the base stack:
overlay_filament|base_filament@0.20+next_base@0.16
Thicknesses are formatted to two decimal places. Profiles need a filament_id for a correction to match. _interpolate_correction is anchored to a factor of one at zero thickness and holds the last correction value beyond the measured range.
compute_pair_corrections is not defined here. Calibration produces those artifacts in calibration/fitting/fitter_core.py; Generator loaders consume the published result.
to_srgb(T_linear, gamma=2.2) is a plain gamma-2.2 compatibility helper with no current production caller. Do not confuse it with the exact piecewise sRGB conversion used elsewhere.
Adjacent-layer geometry (lib/stack_geometry.py)
collapse_adjacent_layers merges adjacent runs of the same filament while preserving order. Non-adjacent repeats remain separate. It is live in Generator appearance prediction, the photo-stack predictor, and Calibration physical-stack prediction.
canonicalize_filament_stack zips parallel filament/thickness arrays and applies that collapse; it is live in Calibration fitting. unzip_layers currently has test callers but no production caller.
Filament registry accessor (lib/filaments.py)
load_registry, list_filament_ids, and get_filament are thin, uncached readers over an explicitly supplied registry path. get_filament injects the requested filament_id into the returned record.
These helpers are not the current app catalog boundary: the current whole-repo callers are tests. Generator and Calibration use their application/model-library loaders instead.
Camera Transform artifact (lib/camera_transform.py)
The Camera Transform bridges model-domain RGB and display sRGB:

forward F: model RGB to display sRGB through root-polynomial features and monotone channel curves;
inverse G: display sRGB to model RGB, baked by Calibration into a 33 × 33 × 33 × 3 LUT and sampled by Generator with trilinear interpolation.

The artifact root uses a CURRENT pointer to select one generation. A generation contains camera_transform.json, inverse_lut_33.npz, and manifest.json. Loaders reject unsafe CURRENT paths, verify manifest hashes, validate schema/shape/finiteness, and cache a single resolved artifact by path plus modification time.
The accepted fit payload uses schema camera_transform_v1, model version v2, 48 finite parameters, ten channel-curve knots, and no lattice. apply_forward evaluates F. invert_forward performs the analytic/Newton inverse during Calibration LUT baking. Generator ingress does not run Newton iteration; it calls load_inverse_lut and apply_inverse_lut.
In packaged-library mode, Generator resolves these artifacts inside the selected immutable published model library. Compatibility data-root fallback remains relevant only outside that mode.
Stable source anchors

Prisma/lib/transmission.py: linear_to_oklab, oklab_to_linear, build_spline, predict, compose
Prisma/lib/color.py: scalar color helpers
Prisma/lib/stack_geometry.py: adjacent-layer utilities
Prisma/lib/filaments.py: test/reference registry accessor
Prisma/lib/camera_transform.py: artifact validation and F/G execution
Prisma/generator/model.py: live target conversion wrappers
Prisma/generator/appearance_model.py: live stack-geometry consumer
Prisma/calibration/fitting/color_math.py: live Calibration color-math duplicate

Related: The Transmission Model, Model-domain ingress and display conversion, Camera Transform, generator.model, generator.pipeline.staged.orchestration, and generator.pipeline.staged_runner.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Model-domain ingress and display conversion
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: the product solve converts the prepared display-sRGB source through the published Camera Transform inverse LUT before constructing its model-OKLab targets, while display-facing prediction artifacts pass model-domain predictions through the matching forward transform.

This page records the two live domain boundaries. For the conceptual model, see Model-domain ingress and Camera Transform.
Domain flow
loaded, framed, adjusted, and optionally preprocessed display-sRGB raster
  → Camera Transform inverse LUT G
  → model-domain RGB
  → OKLab target cloud (domain = model_oklab)
  → gamut handling and staged solve
The reverse, display-only boundary is:
model-domain prediction
  → Camera Transform forward transform F
  → display-encoded sRGB PNG
predicted.png and target_transmission.png are model/transmission-domain images encoded for storage as PNGs. predicted_appearance.png and predicted_color_only_appearance.png are forward-transformed display-appearance images.
Ingress ownership
pipeline.target_cloud.compute_solve_target_cloud is the single target-cloud owner shared by live solving and automatic palette suggestion. It calls model.image_to_target, converts the result to OKLab, and projects the observation grid onto the solve grid. Its SolveTargetCloud carries the observation and solve clouds, both shapes, the fixed model_oklab domain identifier, and ingress provenance.
When model_domain_ingress is true, image_to_target loads and samples the configured inverse LUT. The current server calls _force_mandatory_product_settings at product boundaries, so ingress is mandatory in the web product. Lower-level compatibility constructors still expose false defaults, but false is not a current selectable product mode.
This conversion is not the first operation on the uploaded file. Source framing, resampling, ordinary image adjustments, and any enabled F1 preprocessing operators occur before target-cloud construction.
Published Camera Transform contract
lib.camera_transform.load_camera_transform loads the forward transform and load_inverse_lut loads G. A transform root may contain multiple generation directories, with CURRENT selecting exactly one. The loaders reject an absolute or multi-component pointer, verify the generation manifest’s SHA-256 values, and then validate the selected artifacts.
The accepted forward payload has:

schema camera_transform_v1;
model version v2;
used_lattice=false;
48 finite parameters;
ten monotone-curve knots per channel.

The inverse LUT must be finite and have shape (33, 33, 33, 3). Missing, malformed, incompatible, or hash-mismatched artifacts raise CameraTransformError; Generator does not silently fall back to gamma-only ingress.
apply_inverse_lut accepts an integer image by normalizing it to [0, 1], clamps LUT coordinates, performs trilinear interpolation, and returns float32 model-domain RGB.
Display artifact baking
After a solve, the server writes the normal model-domain predicted.png, then calls model_domain_display.bake_view_domain_images:

recover model-domain linear RGB from Generator’s gamma-2.2 PNG encoding;
apply F with apply_appearance_transform;
write predicted_appearance.png directly as display-encoded sRGB.

For the source-side transmission comparison, the helper applies G to the prepared source and writes target_transmission.png with the model-domain PNG encoder. It returns the transform path and SHA-256, which the server stores in run metadata.
The recipe viewer also calls bake_appearance_png for predicted_color_only_appearance.png. SolveResult.predict_image_color_only zeroes the variable white-cap maps—total, boundary, and detail—then reuses the normal prediction path. The white base remains. In a swap-banded solve, fixed commutative white fill supplied by the band plan also remains; “color only” means removal of the variable cap, not removal of every possible white contribution.
The UI prefers the appearance artifacts for display while retaining the model-domain artifacts for diagnostics.
Runtime boundaries and provenance

The published library’s CURRENT generation pins F and G together; loaders cache by resolved path plus modification time.
Target construction records domain="model_oklab"; gamut mapping and candidate distances operate on that cloud rather than on display-sRGB pixels.
appearance_model.py’s appearance-named prediction methods are compatibility pass-throughs after projection-slot retirement. Display conversion belongs to this ingress/display boundary.
Calibration calls invert_forward while baking the inverse LUT. Generator’s hot ingress path only samples the baked LUT.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Image preprocessing the F1 slot
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
Image preprocessing—the F1 slot

In one sentence: F1 runs an ordered chain of enabled image operators after profiles are loaded and before solve-target construction, converting declared color domains at boundaries, validating every returned raster, and optionally publishing view-only previews.

The runner is preprocessing/runner.py; public data types are in preprocessing/types.py; conversions are in preprocessing/color_convert.py. Operator behavior is documented on Preprocessing operators.
Placement in a live solve
pipeline.runner.run_pipeline owns the sequence:
load profiles
  → optionally resolve F2 palette metadata
  → run F1 preprocessing
  → compute_solve_target_cloud(post-preprocess raster)
  → LUT/gamut work
  → staged backend
The facade resolves enabled operators from persisted module state and places their instances on PipelineConfig.preprocessors. If the list is empty, run_pipeline skips the whole F1 block and the original raster continues unchanged.
Runner contract
run_preprocessing_pipeline:

sorts instances by (order, fully-qualified class name);
validates that a non-empty chain ends in srgb_u8 or srgb_f32 before any operator runs;
infers ingress as srgb_u8 for uint8 or srgb_f32 for float32;
converts the current raster to each operator’s declared input domain;
calls apply, validates the result, and records a trace step;
collects debug maps under <module_name>:<map_name>;
optionally publishes a display-safe preview without replacing the chain raster.

It returns (postprocess_image, trace, debug_maps). An empty chain returns the original object plus empty trace/debug collections.
Sorting
_sort_operators uses the numeric order first and the fully-qualified class name as a deterministic tie breaker. Filesystem discovery is independently lexical; it does not supply the execution tie order.
Active operators use the 100–199, 200–299, and 300–399 order ranges.
Chain and result validation
_validate_chain rejects a last operator whose declared output is not sRGB. This happens before the first apply call, so the chain cannot partially run before that error.
After each call, _validate_apply_result checks:

the return value is PreprocessingResult;
image is a NumPy array;
image height and width match the input;
the returned output-domain name is known;
dtype matches that returned domain;
every output value is finite.

These failures raise PreprocessingContractError and name the offending operator. Operator-specific parameter/context failures may still raise their own exception types—for example, C1/C2 explicitly raise ValueError if required palette metadata is absent.
Each successful PreprocessingTraceStep records module name, input/output domains, a copy of metrics, and cache_hit=False. F1 itself does not cache operator outputs. Trace and debug maps are written to PipelineState; the similarly named preprocessing_metrics field is not populated by this runner.
Color domains and conversion






























DomainDtype/rangeMeaningsrgb_u8uint8 [0,255]Display-encoded sRGBsrgb_f32float32, nominally [0,1]Normalized display-encoded sRGBlinear_rgb_f32float32, nominally [0,1]Linear-light sRGB primaries; temporary out-of-range values are allowedoklab_f32float32D65 OKLab
_convert directly handles the six edges between srgb_f32 and the other three domains. Any other pair is composed through srgb_f32; for example, linear RGB to OKLab becomes linear RGB → sRGB → OKLab.
The sRGB transfer is the IEC 61966-2-1 piecewise function, not Generator’s separate gamma-2.2 PNG approximation. sRGB/linear helpers are sign-preserving and do not clamp. Conversion to srgb_u8 clips and rounds. The OKLab inverse delegates to lib.transmission.oklab_to_linear, which clips to the RGB cube; therefore an OKLab round trip is not an unclipped HDR-preserving path.
The runner owns the initial conversion as well as inter-operator conversions. Operators should not normalize their own input behind the contract.
Context and F2 palette metadata
One frozen PreprocessingContext is built per F1 execution with the current config, an image fingerprint, the original pre-F1 source raster, source_path=None, and optional palette metadata.
resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain runs only if at least one enabled operator declares "palette_metadata" in required_context. If none does, the shared context contains None. If any operator opts in, the single resolved object is present on the shared context passed to every operator; required_context is the opt-in trigger, not a per-operator visibility filter. Palette-blind operators are expected simply not to consume it.
Preview publication
With a snapshot publisher, every successful operator output is converted to srgb_u8 and published as preprocess/<module_name>. That conversion is view-only: the next operator receives the unpreviewed result in its declared domain.
For an operator that declares the palette-metadata requirement, the preview key also incorporates the metadata request fingerprint. This prevents a palette-aware preview from colliding with the same operator’s preview under a different envelope.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Palette metadata
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: F2 samples an approximate historical-spline color envelope for the current palette and white sandwich, then supplies its lightness endpoints and hue/lightness chroma ceilings to the C1 and C2 preprocessing operators.

Live wiring and model boundary
F2 runs inside pipeline.runner.run_pipeline, before F1 preprocessing and target-cloud construction. resolve_palette_metadata_for_chain is called once only when at least one enabled operator requests palette_metadata; otherwise it returns None.
The implementation is important: F2 calls lib.transmission.compose over ProfileSet spline profiles. It does not use the active photo-stack v2 appearance provider, even when that provider is selected for solving. The runner records this provenance as historical_profile_compose. F2 is therefore an approximate conditioning envelope based on the published historical profiles, not a promise that it reproduces the exact active v2 solve gamut.
The one resolved PaletteMetadata object is placed on the shared PreprocessingContext. C1 and C2 are the current opt-in operators.
Output shape
PaletteMetadata is frozen and contains:













































FieldShapeMeaningachievable_black_oklab(3,) float32Sampled point with minimum OKLab Lachievable_white_oklab(3,) float32Sampled point with maximum OKLab Lmax_chroma_by_hue(12,) float32Sampled maximum chroma in each 30° hue binhue_degrees(12,) float32Hue-bin centersl_bin_centers(8,) float32Lightness-bin centers spanning the sampled L endpointsmax_chroma_by_hue_l(12,8) float32Served hue/lightness chroma ceilingrequest_fingerprint32 hex charactersTruncated SHA-256 of the normalized request
C1 consumes the black/white L endpoints. C2 prefers the 2-D hue/lightness ceiling and retains the 1-D hue ceiling as a compatibility fallback.
Request and fingerprint
PaletteMetadataRequest.from_config includes the fields that the implementation treats as envelope-relevant:

palette IDs, sorted as an unordered set;
white-base and effective white-cap IDs;
base, minimum-cap, and effective maximum-cap thicknesses;
total-height budget, k_max, and layer height;
correction enablement and a stable serialization of the correction payload.

It excludes solver weights, gamut mode, image resolution, grouping controls, and preprocessing parameters.
The fingerprint identifies this normalized request, not the mathematical envelope itself. Two differently named/profiled inputs that happened to produce identical sampled points would still have different request fingerprints.
Envelope sampling
For each of three nominal cap samples—minimum, midpoint, maximum, deduplicated when equal—_candidate_oklab_points composes:

the bare white-base/white-cap sandwich;
each single color when thickness budget permits;
every two-filament combination if k_max >= 2;
every three-filament combination if k_max >= 3.

Each stack obeys d_wb + color thicknesses + d_wc <= t_max. Enabled pair corrections are passed to compose.
The per-color sample count is selected adaptively from 4 through 8. _adaptive_samples_per_layer chooses the largest count whose estimated candidate population is no more than 40,000; if even four exceeds that budget, four is still used as a hard fidelity floor.
Despite _layer_sample_thicknesses’s current “snapped” docstring, the implementation uses np.linspace(layer_height, budget, n_samples) and does not quantize every sample to an integral layer count. Layer height controls the maximum sample count and lower endpoint, while the final sample is the remaining continuous budget. This is an envelope approximation rather than an enumeration of only printable discrete stacks.
The sampled transmissions are converted to OKLab. The resolver selects the minimum- and maximum-L points, computes maximum chroma per hue bin, and builds a hue × lightness grid. Empty lightness cells are filled by interpolation within each hue row, then a three-cell max dilation along lightness preserves nearby peaks. It never dilates across hue.
The no-points fallback is defensive and normally unreachable because every cap sample adds a bare white sandwich. If reached, it returns the minimum-cap white point for both endpoints with zero chroma ceilings.
C1 and C2 behavior




















OperatorConsumptionMissing/degenerate behaviorC1 achievable tonemapRemaps source OKLab L toward sampled black/white L endpointsMissing metadata raises ValueError; collapsed endpoints return identity with a degenerate metricC2 soft gamut compressInterpolates a hue/lightness chroma bound and applies hue-preserving soft-knee compressionMissing metadata raises ValueError; empty or effectively zero ceilings return identity
Users do not configure F2 directly. Enabling C1 or C2 triggers it. The selected palette, white sandwich, height budget, layer limit, and correction settings determine the request.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Palette suggestion search and ranking
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
In one sentence: palette suggestion precomputes nearest distances to single/pair gamut clouds, searches exact-size filament subsets exhaustively or by multi-start greedy refinement, enforces distinct alternatives, and sparsely rescores the bounded finalists with three-color gamuts.

Signature and gamut construction are documented on Automatic palette suggestion. This page follows the current generator/palette/suggest.py search contract.
One thorough search path
suggest_palettes has no search_mode. It prepares a _PaletteSearchContext and always calls _thorough_search. Legacy search_mode and quality_weights fields are rejected by the server payload.
_prepare_palette_search_context:

filters unsupported/excluded filaments;
asserts signature/gamut domain equality;
chooses robust ranking for a supplied model backend and mean ranking otherwise;
builds/caches single clouds;
precomputes one nearest-distance vector per single and pair cloud.

Each trial palette can then be scored by elementwise minima over small arrays rather than by rebuilding gamut clouds and KDTrees.
Exhaustive versus multi-start
_thorough_search computes C(n_available, requested_size):

at or below 500,000 combinations, _exhaustive_search evaluates all sets;
above 500,000, _multi_start_search uses multiple seeded greedy builds and local swaps.

The exhaustive path scores combinations in chunks of 2,048. It keeps a bounded best-candidate buffer rather than every candidate indefinitely.
The multi-start path ranks individual-filament seeds, uses up to the best eight as starts, greedily adds one filament at a time, then performs up to 20 local-swap passes. If those starts converge to too few distinct sets, it expands scored single-swap neighbors through a frontier until the candidate buffer is sufficiently populated or no new neighbors remain.
Ranking objective
_score_palette_metrics returns:

weighted mean distance;
maximum distance;
weighted percentage above the 0.02 OKLab coverage threshold;
weighted 90th percentile.

_palette_rank_score maps those to one scalar:

















ModeObjectivemeanmean_derobustmean_de + 0.35·p90_de + 0.15·max_de + 0.03·(pct_above/100)
Robust mode penalizes poorly covered color regions that a mean alone can hide. It is the current photo-stack model path; historical spline suggestion uses mean mode.
The deterministic sort key is rank score, mean, maximum, then sorted filament IDs.
Distinctness and diversity
_select_diverse_candidates never returns a duplicate filament set. It first prefers a set differing from each already-selected set by at least two replaced members (symmetric-difference size at least four). If that preference would return fewer than requested, it fills best-first from rejected but still distinct sets.
The intended product contract is N requested means N distinct palettes when the available/searchable pool permits it. Equality is by filament set, not order or downstream thickness recipe.
Exact-size browser contract
The browser sends one exact n_filaments value. _thorough_search evaluates
only that size and returns no more than top_k distinct palettes. The server
does not clamp the request to printer capacity and does not search a size
ladder. If fewer supported eligible candidates remain than the requested
size, the request fails clearly rather than returning undersized palettes.
Printer capacity is therefore presentation and solve-planning context, not a
suggestion search boundary. An oversized request receives the same exact-size
search and a live browser warning that a solve may require filament swaps.
Actual grouping depends on solve-time recipe use, so Auto-Suggest does not
claim a swap count.
Sparse three-color finalist rescore
suggest_palettes_detailed first selects the exact-size finalists using the
single/pair search. It then rescales that same bounded set—at most the requested
top_k—with sparse three-color gamut samples.
For every triple contained in those finalists, it builds a sparse triple cloud (four color-thickness samples per filament, cap step eight), precomputes centroid distances, and rescales each finalist’s distance vector with the new minima. It then:

reranks the exact-size finalist set;
adds timing/finalist-count provenance.

It does not reopen the exhaustive/multi-start search with triple distances, and
it does not evaluate triples for non-finalist palettes. The public
list-returning suggest_palettes wrapper uses the same detailed exact-size path.
Endpoint behavior
The server builds common arguments from the active white sandwich, model exclusions, coverage threshold, target metric weight, and active appearance provider, then calls the detailed exact-size search.
Suggestion runs in a background worker with job-qualified status and cancellation. Progress is monotonic at the server boundary; expensive gamut loops check the cancellation callback between units of work.
