prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Color Solver settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The Color Solver section governs the core of a solve: the color model, how target colors are prepared and matched to filament recipes, and how the image is partitioned into color regions. Two closely related controls — Solve Pitch (resolution) and Solve Mode — sit at the top of the Essentials section in the app but are documented here, since they set the solve’s resolution and cap strategy. For the mechanism behind these stages, see The Solve.
Solver core
Solve Pitch — default 0.20 mm; the displayed minimum follows the active nozzle diameter. This is the physical spacing of the solve grid: the distance between points for which the solver chooses recipes. Smaller values preserve more detail but increase solve and export cost roughly with the square of the resolution. Image Width and Height must resolve to whole cells. Prisma uses half-up rounding for cell counts, so 100.2 mm at 0.4 mm becomes 251 cells and a 100.4 mm resolved image area. The Image page warns immediately when either axis is not aligned; Print Size and Rendered Size reflect the resolved grid. At solve time the backend returns the authoritative geometry. Continuing through the size-adjustment confirmation writes those resolved dimensions into the Image fields, switches the aspect control to W×H, and verifies alignment before the solve starts. Direct API solves do not require a browser confirmation but use the same canonical grid.
Prisma does not silently raise Solve Pitch after a nozzle change. When the user starts a solve with a pitch below the active nozzle diameter, the frontend offers to set it to that exact diameter and continue; accepting uses the normal settings path and preserves the physical cap-smoothing radius. Equality and coarser pitches remain valid. The backend solve-start gate independently rejects an unresolved mismatch. Dimension alignment is recalculated after any accepted nozzle-pitch correction.
Solve Mode — Color (default) or Luminance. It changes how the white cap is built and — indirectly — the color recipes. In Color, the cap realizes the brightness the color solve already chose. In Luminance, the cap is reconstructed from the image’s own luminance and carries the photo’s tone and fine detail as white relief; because that reserves part of the height budget for the cap, the recipe table is built over a narrower range of cap thicknesses, so the solver can pick different per-filament recipes than in Color mode. Solve Mode is a preset: selecting Luminance reconfigures several White Cap fields at once — it reveals Shading balance and forces the boundary cap to its smooth form. See Solve Modes and White Cap settings.
Appearance Model — Color Model v1 or Color Model v2 (default). The forward color model used to predict stacks, build the recipe table, render previews, and score accuracy. Color Model v1 is the spline/multiplicative transmission model. Color Model v2 is the interaction-aware photo-stack model and requires the corresponding runtime bundle from the active published model library. A valid published library supplies the artifacts Prisma needs for the offered models. See Appearance provider.
Recipe Search
This subsection controls how target colors are prepared and matched to filament recipes. Most fields are advanced.
Out-of-gamut handling (advanced) — Nearest reachable color (default) or Preserve hue. How target colors the palette cannot reproduce are moved before recipe lookup. Both modes use the same unweighted distance to the nearest discrete recipe-table sample to decide whether a target exceeds Color mismatch tolerance. Nearest reachable color moves geometrically outside targets toward the reachable color hull in full three-dimensional OKLab, so lightness and hue can shift before the final recipe lookup. Preserve hue scales the target’s two chroma axes together toward neutral, preserving hue while reducing chroma and moving lightness only as needed to enter the printable range. See Gamut mapping.
White-point rescale — default off. Rescales every target so the source’s white maps to the print’s actual paper white (the thinnest white stack), keeping pale tints in gamut instead of clipping them to white. Predicted previews read slightly darker and warmer when it is on. An enabled run also reports White-point rescale: On in the solve-card settings summary.
Color corrections — default on. Applies calibrated correction data while the recipe table is built — pair corrections for Color Model v1, the correction layer for Color Model v2. For Color Model v1 it only takes effect when Max colors per region is at least 2.
Max colors per region — 1–7 in the browser, default 3. The most distinct colored filaments a single region’s recipe may stack. Higher values can match colors more closely but multiply the recipe search; the effective cap is the smaller of this and the palette size. The frontend enforces the 1–7 range, but the backend’s generic config payload accepts an arbitrary integer and does not repeat that upper-bound check for direct API callers.
Color mismatch tolerance (advanced) — default 0.01, in OKLab color difference. A target farther than this from the nearest discrete recipe-table sample is flagged as out of gamut. Preserve hue then searches its hue-preserving path for an improvement. Nearest reachable color projects the target only when it is also geometrically outside the continuous hull; a flagged point already inside the hull stays in place and the final recipe lookup handles the remaining discrete mismatch. Lower is stricter. The 0.01–0.20 shown is a guide, not an enforced limit.
Chroma weight (advanced) — default 1.0. Weights chroma against lightness when matching recipes: above 1 favors hue and saturation over brightness, below 1 favors brightness. It changes which recipe is chosen, not the reported color error, which is always measured in unweighted OKLab. The current logarithmic slider spans 0.125–8.0.
Region Construction
This subsection controls how the image is divided into color-planning regions and how those regions are refined. Every field except Color region target is advanced.
Region method (advanced) — Image regions (default), Superpixels, or Fixed grid. How the image is partitioned into initial color regions before recipes are chosen. The image-aware modes follow image structure; Fixed grid uses uniform square cells.
Region planning scale (advanced) — 1–4× in the browser, default 1. Plans the regions on a grid coarsened by this factor. Higher values make broader, simpler regions that solve faster but follow fine edges less closely. The staged helper clamps direct values only to a minimum of 1, so the browser’s upper bound is not a generic backend constraint.
Color region target — default 0.60 mm. The target physical width of the initial regions: smaller follows image structure more closely, larger makes broader, simpler regions. Note that this value is raised to a printability-derived minimum, so entering a value below that minimum has no further effect. This is the only always-visible field in the subsection.
Neutral-field protection (advanced) — default Off. Reduces false hue boundaries in low-chroma fields by reconsidering adjacent region recipes when the source regions are already perceptually similar. The modes control the maximum source chroma admitted to that reconsideration: Narrow 0.010, Standard 0.020, and Broad 0.035 in OKLab. Source neighbors must also be within 0.018 dE. The optimizer penalizes excessive output discontinuity and excessive recipe chroma while allowing at most 0.004 additional local mean dE over the original region choice. Broad therefore covers pale and subtly colored subjects as well as neutral backgrounds; it should be checked carefully on brightly lit pale skin. The setting is opt-in and participates in settings profiles, solved-run snapshots, and solve-cache invalidation.
This control only chooses among recipes already present in each region’s Stage 2 candidate frontier. It cannot synthesize a neutral recipe that the palette cannot print or that candidate generation did not retain.
Local recipe corrections (advanced) — default on. Lets individual grid cells inside a broader region adopt a better-matching recipe when the color improvement is strong enough. This preserves fine detail at the cost of more small recipe patches.
Boundary mutation (advanced) — default on in the current product configuration. Lets the solver redraw recipe boundaries between neighbors when borrowing a neighbor’s recipe lowers local color error. Turning it off disables that refinement. When enabled, the UI reveals four tuning fields:

Mutation passes — 1–16, default 1. Each pass can move a boundary by one more solve-grid cell. Prisma stops early when a pass accepts no pixels.
Mutation current-dE percentile — empty/off by default. When set, only boundary candidates whose current color error is at or above this percentile are eligible. The threshold is recomputed from the current candidates on each pass.
Mutation min gain — empty by default, which uses 0.010 dE. Candidate pixels are grouped into connected patches that share the same original and borrowed recipes; the patch’s mean improvement must exceed this threshold.
Mutation min contact — empty by default, meaning at least one solve-grid pixel of shared boundary with the donor recipe. A supplied millimeter value is converted to ceil(value / Solve Pitch) contact pixels.

The older Mutation grouping control is not present in the current UI or config contract. Boundary mutation already evaluates four-connected patch components and records its component/contact diagnostics internally.
The result of this section is the per-cell recipe map that the white cap, grouping, and export stages build on.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Geometry settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The Essentials section holds the print’s physical envelope — total height budget, layer grid, base plate, and the white base/cap filament — together with the two headline solver controls, Solve Mode and Solve Pitch (covered in Color Solver settings). This page documents the geometry controls. They are used throughout later stages: they define how much room the color layers and white cap have, and the layer grid everything is quantized to. None are advanced; all are always visible. A cross-section diagram in the panel shows how they relate — base at the bottom (light enters here), color layers above, white cap on top, all within the maximum total thickness.
Stack Geometry
Max Total Thickness — default 3.0 mm; the UI suggests 1.0–5.0 mm. The hard ceiling on the finished object’s height, counting base, color layers, and cap together. Everything else is fitted underneath it: the white cap is clamped so base + color + cap never exceeds this value, and the color-layer budget is whatever remains after the base and the minimum cap are reserved. Raising it gives the solver more layers to work with; lowering it forces thinner stacks.
Layer Height — default 0.08 mm; the displayed supported range follows the active nozzle (0.04–0.20 mm when no nozzle data is available). This is the thickness of one printed layer and the quantization step for the whole stack: color layers, white cap, and detail relief are all whole multiples of it. It must match the layer height set in your slicer exactly. In the browser, a value outside the active nozzle’s supported range appears in the validation block and prevents a solve from starting.
White Base/Cap Filament — the white filament used for both the solid base plate (the surface light enters through) and the viewing-side cap. As the base it is the first layer in every stack, so its transmission underlies all the color above it; the same filament forms the white cap over the top. The list is stricter than “has a fitted profile”: the filament must also be available in the active model generation, not excluded, and explicitly marked eligible for white-cap use.
Base Thickness — default 0.20 mm; the UI suggests 0.08–1.0 mm. The thickness of the base plate. It is subtracted from the total height budget before color and cap are sized, so a thicker base leaves fewer layers for color.
The read-out below the table reports the resulting color-layer budget. The browser’s solve preflight requires a positive color budget and requires the remainder after base and minimum cap to be allocatable in whole layer-height steps. The validation block proposes the nearest lower and higher total thicknesses when it is not. These alignment errors, an unsupported layer height, and a Solve Pitch below the nozzle diameter all block the normal browser start action; the broader 1–5 mm and 0.08–1.0 mm ranges are suggestions rather than hard limits.
This validation is not symmetric across every API layer. The backend independently repeats the Solve Pitch versus nozzle-diameter check, but it does not currently repeat the browser’s nozzle layer-height range or whole-layer budget checks at job admission. Direct API/developer callers therefore must not treat the browser-only checks as a backend guarantee; lower-level effective_max_layers() simply truncates the available color budget to an integer layer count.
For how the base layer enters the optical model, see The Transmission Model; for how the cap consumes the remaining budget, see White Cap.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Grouping settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
There is no user-selectable grouping method in the current generator. When a full solve’s color palette fits within the available AMS color slots, no swap grouping is created. When it does not fit, the pipeline automatically runs a bounded scout and deterministic swap-band planner; the resulting plan is exposed in the solve result and used by export and swap-instruction endpoints.
The old Greedy Optimize and Group Budget settings described here previously belonged to the deleted pluggable grouping subsystem. They are not current UI controls or production solver paths.
When automatic grouping runs
The live trigger is:
FULL_PRESET
and no nested swap-banding scout run
and len(palette) > color_slots()
color_slots() is the total AMS slot count minus the effective white-slot count. The check is made by _swap_banding_requested in pipeline/runner.py, before the normal LUT build. The server independently evaluates the same palette-versus-slot condition when choosing its solve progress route. The preview preset does not enter this full-solve swap-banding route.
Planning contract
The first pass is a bounded, unbanded scout. _downsample_swap_scout_image limits its long side to 384 pixels, so the scout can estimate material usage without changing the main solve raster. The planner then calls choose_band_plan in grouping/band_plan.py with the canonical palette, scout thickness maps, color-slot capacity, layer height, and available color-layer budget.
choose_band_plan:

refuses palettes larger than ten colors (MAX_EXHAUSTIVE_FILAMENTS = 10);
enumerates constrained partitions in canonical order, with at most color_slots colors per band;
estimates each band’s height from the 99th percentile of its scout usage (BAND_HEIGHT_QUANTILE = 0.99);
chooses the candidate with the smallest total raw band layers, then lowest predicted white-fill volume, then canonical partition order; and
clamps the selected band layers to the available color-layer budget when necessary.

choose_band_plan returns a frozen BandPlan containing the canonical palette, groups, band-layer budgets, usage statistics, and whether clamping occurred. The runner serializes that choice into a plain swap_grouping metadata dictionary on PipelineState and in diagnostics; the facade copies it into SolveResult. The normal solve then uses the corresponding banded LUT route and white-fill calculations. Downstream export validates this persisted choice instead of recomputing a new grouping.
White fill and export
Each band’s color stack is assigned an exact whole-layer height. band_fill_thicknesses and band_fill_maps derive the white fill as:
assigned band layers × layer height − color thickness
Negative fill is rejected. The white fill is therefore a derived carrier for exact band height; it is not a user-selected grouping setting and does not represent an independent color recipe.
The export path validates the persisted plan rather than inferring groups from final maps. It writes fixed-slot band metadata, generates swap instructions, and inserts M600 pauses where required. The plan is also used by preview reconstruction and solve summaries. If the plan is absent, the ordinary single-load export path is used.
What remains user-controlled
Users control the inputs that determine whether grouping is needed:

the palette membership and therefore its size (the solve canonicalizes members into dark-first order);
the active printer’s AMS slot count and reserved white slots; and
palette membership and size, including the exact Palette colors request used by Auto-Suggest.

Those controls do not select a grouping algorithm. A palette exceeding the available color slots may require swaps; the solve and export paths decide the deterministic grouping plan.
Related

AMS grouping and swap planning — the full scout, partition, export, and instruction lifecycle.
Pipeline Map — where the swap-banding expansion enters the five-phase spine.
The staged backend (Stage 0-5) — the solver stages that consume the banded plan.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Pre-processing settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
Pre-processing conditions the source image before the color solver sees it. It has two parts: how the image is resampled onto the solve grid, and an ordered chain of optional modules that clean or reshape it. For the mechanism behind these operations, see Preprocessing.
Source Sampling
Resample kernel (advanced) — default Lanczos. The filter used when the source image is scaled down to the solve resolution. Lanczos is sharper and preserves detail but can ring at hard edges; Area integrates over each destination pixel for a softer, more anti-aliased result, better suited to coarse print-scale solves. It acts only when the source is larger than the solve grid — the image is never upscaled — so on a small source it does nothing. The current setting is source_resample_kernel.
Pre-processing Modules
The modules run on the image just before solving, in a fixed order: Noise Reduction → Print-Scale Smoothing → Flat-Area Smoothing → Palette Tone Fit → Palette Saturation Fit. Each is toggled independently. All five operator classes default to disabled. The live toggle snapshot is mutable Generator Workspace data at config/modules.json; if that file does not yet exist, the loader materializes the registered class defaults in memory. A user or Settings Profile can persist a different snapshot, and that live Workspace state is the control plane used at solve time. The similarly named checked-in Prisma/generator/app/modules.json is not the production state file. Discovery, normalization, persistence, and execution are documented in Preprocessing operators.
Each module is set with a named preset (strength levels plus Off and Custom); choosing Custom exposes the individual fields listed below. The first three clean and simplify the image so color regions come out less fragmented. The two palette-aware modules reshape the image toward what the selected palette can reproduce and require palette metadata.
Noise Reduction
Off by default. An edge-preserving (bilateral) blur that softens small noise so it does not splinter the image into many tiny color regions, while keeping edges intact.

Filter radius (1–8) — the blur window size; larger covers more area.
Color similarity (0.005–0.25) — how different two colors can be and still be averaged together; higher blurs across stronger color differences.
Spatial reach (0.5–10) — how far, in pixels, the blur extends.

Print-Scale Smoothing
Off by default. A bilateral blur tuned to the scale the printer can actually resolve, producing simpler, larger color regions. Its physical reach is derived from the nozzle diameter and the solve pitch, so changing either changes its strength.

Feature scale (0.5–2.0) — multiplies the print-feature blur radius; below 1 keeps more detail, above 1 flattens more.
Color similarity (0.005–0.25) — the color-difference threshold for blurring, as above.
Passes (1–3) — how many times the blur is applied.

Flat-Area Smoothing
Off by default. A total-variation flatten that collapses gradual texture into broad flat areas, giving a more painted or graphic look at higher strengths.

Flattening strength (0.005–0.40) — how aggressively texture is flattened.
Scale strength to print width (on/off) — ties the effective strength to the print-feature scale (nozzle size) so it tracks the printable resolution.
Flattening mode — which color axes are flattened: Lightness only, Lightness and chroma, or RGB channels.
Iteration limit (2–500, default 100) — caps the number of iterations used to compute the flatten. Low caps can stop well before convergence; 2 is the first effective value.

Palette Tone Fit
Off by default. Requires a palette. Remaps the image’s tonal range, in perceptual lightness, toward the darkest and lightest the selected palette can physically print, so shadows and highlights land where the filaments can reach. It anchors on source shadow and highlight percentiles and blends the result in by a chosen amount.

Tone fit strength (0–1) — how strongly the remap is applied (0 = none, 1 = full).
Shadow anchor (0–10) — the source lightness percentile treated as black.
Highlight anchor (90–100) — the source lightness percentile treated as white; must sit above the shadow anchor.
Midtone curve (0.5–2.0) — bends the curve between the anchors toward lighter or darker midtones.

Palette Saturation Fit
Off by default. Requires a palette. Softly pulls colors more saturated than the palette can reproduce back toward its per-hue limit, preserving hue and lightness, using a smooth knee rather than a hard clip.

Compression start (0.50–1.00) — the fraction of the palette’s hue-local saturation limit at which compression begins; lower starts earlier and affects more pixels.
Compression softness (0.05–1.50) — how gradual the knee is.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/Technical Reference/Using/Settings/White Cap settings.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: White Cap settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The White Cap section governs the white layer built over the color stack — the surface the print is viewed through. It sets the cap’s minimum thickness, how the boundary cap (the closed white surface) is constructed, and the detail relief above it. The white filament itself is the shared White Base/Cap Filament, chosen in the Essentials section. For the mechanism, see White Cap.
The Solve Mode setting (in Color Solver settings) strongly affects this section. In Luminance mode the boundary cap follows source luminance: the Boundary cap selector is hidden and forced to its smooth form, and the Luminance-only Shading balance field appears. See Solve Modes.
Min Cap Layers — default 2, minimum 1. The minimum number of white layers in the cap, counted in printed layers (its millimeter thickness is this count times the layer height). The cap is never thinner than this anywhere.
Boundary
The boundary cap is the closed white surface that covers the color stack; its thickness sets how bright each region reads.
Boundary cap (advanced) — Detail Aware (default) or Smooth. Smooth shapes the boundary cap into one continuous outer surface that carries the tonal relief directly. Detail Aware keeps the boundary cap structural — holding its predicted appearance close to the raw optical cap — and pushes the remaining tonal relief up into the detail cap instead. Hidden and forced to Smooth in Luminance mode.
Appearance budget (advanced) — default 0.004 dE; the UI suggests 0–0.05. (Detail Aware boundary cap only.) The most extra predicted color error, in the color model’s space, allowed as the smoothed boundary candidate departs from the raw optical cap. Candidate pixels over budget fall back toward the raw cap. Lower values preserve the solved appearance more aggressively, at the cost of a busier target surface.
Smoothing radius — default 1.0 mm; the UI suggests 0–20 mm. The physical radius over which the boundary cap’s top surface is smoothed. Internally Prisma converts it to solve-grid cells, so changing Solve Pitch preserves the displayed physical radius. Lower values keep more tonal relief in the surface; higher values produce a cleaner, more contiguous cap. The smoothing is edge-aware — pulled back near strong color and height edges — and the underside still fits the color stack exactly. This field stays active in both solve modes.
Shading balance — default 75. Shown only in Luminance mode. A 0–100 slider (from Detail to Smooth) setting whether the broad luminance shading is carried more by the smooth boundary cap or by fine detail-cap relief. Higher values put more shading in the smooth cap; lower values reserve more for fine detail. The Suggest button proposes a value from the selected image.
Detail
The detail-cap stage is mandatory in both Color and Luminance modes; profiles and API payloads cannot turn the stage off. Its permitted height can still be set to zero with Detail depth, which produces no optional detail relief. Depending on the cap mode, the detail cap carries either the residual of the Detail Aware appearance target or optically selected fine relief above the boundary cap. Its masks then pass through the mandatory printability authoring/gating path.
Detail depth — default 5, minimum 0. The maximum number of whole white detail layers allowed above the boundary cap. It permits height but does not force the cap to use every layer; zero suppresses optional detail height without disabling the mandatory stage. It applies in both solve modes.

prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.title: Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/technical-re.content:
The settings page configures how a solve runs — print geometry, image conditioning, the color solver, the white cap, and material grouping. These are the parameters that rarely change between runs; per-image choices (the source photo, palette, image adjustments, export format) live on the workflow tabs, not here.
Settings are organized into four editable sections, in pipeline order:

Essentials — the print’s physical envelope (total thickness, layer height, base thickness) and the white base/cap filament, plus the two headline solver controls, Solve Mode and Solve Pitch (detailed under Color Solver).
Pre-processing — how the source image is conditioned before solving: resampling onto the solve grid, plus optional smoothing and palette-fit modules.
Color Solver — the color model, the recipe search, and how the image is partitioned into color regions. (Solve Mode and resolution now live in Essentials.)
White Cap — the white layer over the colors: minimum thickness, the boundary cap, and the detail relief. (The white filament is shared with the base, set in Essentials.)

AMS swap grouping is not an editable settings section in the current build. It is created automatically during a full solve only when the palette exceeds the available AMS color slots; see Grouping settings and AMS grouping and swap planning.
Settings profiles
A settings profile is a saved bundle of every editable settings-profile field, the preprocessing parameter map, and the complete current preprocessing-module toggle snapshot. Palette membership, source image, frame/crop state, image adjustments, and export options are not settings-profile fields.
The profile bar names the loaded profile and adds badges for its state:

system is the built-in Basic profile;
startup is the profile selected to load when the app starts;
TEMP is a session-only profile reconstructed from a solved run; and
modified means a profile field or module toggle differs from the snapshot that was loaded.

Save updates a named profile after confirmation. Save As… writes the current values as a new named profile. Profiles… lists profiles and can load, rename, choose a startup profile, delete, restore the system profile, or open Use Settings from Run….
The built-in Basic profile is regenerated from current product defaults when necessary. It cannot be renamed, overwritten, or deleted. Saving a draft based on Basic therefore uses Save As. Named profile names are case-insensitively unique and cannot be blank, carry leading/trailing whitespace, end in a period, use Windows-forbidden filename characters, or reuse the reserved name Basic. If the selected startup profile is missing or invalid at launch, the backend resets the startup selection to Basic.
Loading a profile changes both the flat session config and the separately persisted preprocessing-module state. The frontend applies both locally, sends the config, then sends the module snapshot. If synchronization fails, it attempts to restore the previous local state and sends compensating backend updates once publication has begun. Those calls are coordinated but are not one atomic backend transaction; a failed compensation is logged and a subsequent server refresh is authoritative.
Settings captured by solved runs
Every live solved-run card has a display-only Settings panel. It preserves the same section order as the editable drawer, renders values as text rather than disabled controls, and has its own Advanced: On/Off view. Clicking the card’s Settings button again closes it.
Use These Settings in that panel reconstructs a session-only profile from the solve. The Saved Runs window and Settings Profiles window provide the same operation for a saved run or autosave without loading its image or restoring the solve card. Prisma uses the archived config plus newer solve-start diagnostics and durable recipe/profile metadata when those are present; this keeps current archives exact while retaining compatibility with older archives that recorded less metadata.
Only one reconstructed run profile exists at a time. It is marked TEMP, identifies its source run, and is replaced when settings from another run are used. It can be modified and used immediately, but it is not written to the profile store and cannot be selected as the startup profile. Saving it uses Save As to create a normal named profile.
When switching away from a modified profile, Prisma offers to save the draft, discard it, or cancel the transition. A TEMP profile is subject to the same guard.
Persistence and backend contract
Persistent profiles live as individual JSON records under Generator/Workspace/settings_profiles/. system-default.json is the canonical Basic record; named profiles use generated identifiers rather than display names as filenames. state.json stores the selected startup-profile identifier. Each JSON update is staged and replaced as one file, but a profile update and a separate startup-state change are not a multi-file transaction.
The backend enumerates named JSON files, skips records it cannot normalize, ignores later records that duplicate an already loaded profile identifier, and sorts valid named profiles by display name. It canonicalizes the resolution fields, supplies current defaults for missing profile fields, normalizes the complete module-toggle map against current module descriptors, and drops explicitly retired compatibility keys. This means an older profile can acquire current defaults for settings it never recorded; it is not treated as a byte-for-byte historical solve record.
The profile API separates list/create/update, startup selection, Basic restoration, and deletion. Basic is rejected by update and delete routes. Deleting the selected startup profile resets startup state to Basic. The frontend additionally prevents deletion of the profile currently loaded into the editable drawer until another profile is loaded.
Showing advanced settings
Many fields are hidden by default as advanced. The drawer’s Advanced: On/Off button reveals them across every section. It changes only visibility; it does not alter solve settings and is not stored inside a settings profile. Its state is saved separately in browser local storage, so the editable drawer normally remembers the user’s choice across launches in that browser profile.
The display-only solved-run Settings panel has a separate Advanced toggle. That panel starts with advanced rows hidden each time it is opened and does not change the editable drawer’s stored preference. Throughout this reference, fields noted as advanced are the fields controlled by these views.

prisma-lithophane-generator/index.title: Prisma Lithophane Generator
prisma-lithophane-generator/index.content:
Welcome to the documentation wiki for Prisma Lithophane Generator. Prisma Generator converts a photo into a 3D-printable color lithophane using a photo-specific palette instead of limiting every print to cyan, magenta, yellow, and white. A palette chosen for the particular image can reproduce its colors more accurately.
Organization
This wiki is divided into four sections, each intended to answer a different kind of question:

Getting Started — a quick-start guide that helps you install and run Prisma Generator for the first time. It includes a step-by-step walkthrough of the basics, from choosing an image to printing a lithophane.
How To Use — a user guide covering Prisma Generator’s features and controls. If you are unsure what a setting does, start here.
How It Works — explanations of the concepts and processes behind Prisma Generator. This section describes the ideas without discussing code or their specific implementation.
Technical Reference — code-level documentation describing how those processes are implemented. It is most useful to readers who want to understand or modify Prisma Generator itself.

readme.title: README
readme.content:
This folder is an Obsidian vault and the source of the published docs site. To read it locally: Open folder as vault in Obsidian → choose this Documentation/ folder → start at Prisma Lithophane Generator or Prisma Calibration. On the website, the landing page at / covers the same ground.
Prisma has two portable distribution packages on Windows and Linux. Generator-only is the streamlined option for making lithophanes from a published model library. Suite adds Calibration, which owns the private sample database and working model fits. Calibration can publish a complete immutable library for Generator, but Generator never reads Calibration’s live Workspace. A packaged macOS release is planned for public launch, but it has not yet been built or smoke-tested. The user-facing installation, launcher, folder, and backup guidance lives in each app’s Getting Started section.
Everything here uses built-in Obsidian features only (wikilinks, tags, graph view, backlinks, search) — no community plugins — so the same vault publishes as a static Quartz website without rework.
Structure
Two top-level sections, one per app, each with four tiers:

Getting Started — orientation and a first run.
How It Works — the phenomena and the math, textbook register, no code identifiers.
How To Use — a plain, task-focused user guide.
Technical Reference — the code-level map, including the dual-audience usage overviews (Using/) and the auto-generated Architecture/ module nodes.

The one rule these docs follow
Every unannotated behavior claim is traced to the actual code, not to prior notes or memory. A deliberately future-facing claim must use the RELEASE-INTENT convention below. Technical Reference pages identify stable source files, symbols, routes, and callers so a reader can verify them without relying on line numbers that drift whenever code moves. If an unannotated claim and the code disagree, the code wins—re-audit the callers and fix the page.
Authoring rules (for maintainers and agents)

Never hard-wrap a wikilink or inline-code span across a line break — Obsidian won’t parse it. Don’t hard-wrap body prose at all.
Page basenames must be unique vault-wide (Quartz resolves wikilinks by shortest path; duplicate basenames across sections make links ambiguous). Don’t title a page a case-variant of another page either — slugs collide.
Landing/overview diagrams are generated by scripts/gen_landing_diagrams.py and injected between LANDING-DIAGRAM markers; per-page nav diagrams by scripts/gen_local_nav_diagrams.py; Architecture nodes by scripts/gen_docs_module_graph*.py. Edit the script tables and re-run — never hand-edit the generated blocks.
Screenshot placeholders use the form > [!note] 📸 Screenshot to capture (one shared convention across both apps).
Check links with scripts/check_docs_wikilinks.py (the vault should stay at 0 dangling links).

Source-only editorial annotations
Use HTML comments for notes that belong in the Markdown source but must not appear in Obsidian reading view or on the published Quartz site. Start each comment with one of these labels so its intent is unambiguous:

<!-- RELEASE-INTENT: ... --> — a deliberately future-facing statement expected to be true for a named release or launch. State what must be verified before removing the comment.
<!-- VERIFY: ... --> — a factual claim that is provisional and needs evidence or testing.
<!-- TODO: ... --> — a known placeholder or unfinished content change.
<!-- QUESTION: ... --> — a request for maintainer or agent input.
<!-- EDITORIAL: ... --> — a writing, structure, or Markdown-syntax instruction rather than literal page text.

Keep a visible qualifier such as “coming soon” when a future-facing page might be published before the planned feature or package is actually available. Do not use an invisible comment to conceal a statement that would mislead readers on the currently published site.
Publishing
scripts/sync_docs_to_quartz.py mirrors the vault into the local Quartz clone’s content/ (stripping title-duplicate leading H1s and rewriting folder-index wikilinks on the copy). scripts/publish_docs.py additionally builds and pushes the live site — only run it when the site should actually update.

index.title: Prisma Documentation
index.content:
Prisma is a color lithophane generator: photograph 3D-printed filament swatches to characterize how each filament transmits light, then decompose an image into a stack of filament layers that reproduces its colors when backlit. Both halves of the system are documented here, built from their source code — every technical claim traces to a file:line.
The two apps

Prisma Lithophane Generator — turn a photo into a backlit color lithophane and export print files for a multi-color 3D printer. The Generator-only Windows and Linux packages include a published Standard Model Library.
Prisma Calibration — measure how filaments transmit light on a lightbox, fit personal working models, and publish an immutable model library for the Generator. Calibration is included in the Windows and Linux Suite packages.

The apps deliberately do not share live data. Calibration owns its database, evidence, and current working models. Generator owns its installed published libraries and uses one complete library at a time. Publishing copies Calibration’s exact current models and public filament catalog across that boundary; later Calibration changes cannot alter a library already installed in Generator. A locally fitted generation becomes Generator-usable only through this same publish step (to the Suite’s Generator folder or as an exported library package).
Each app is organized into four tiers:

Getting Started — orientation and a first run.
How It Works — the phenomena and the math.
How To Use — a plain, task-focused user guide (the calibration app’s is still being rebuilt).
Technical Reference — the code-level map, including the usage overviews (Using) and an auto-generated module-import graph under Architecture/.
